In a recent development, black Friday may still be a few weeks away, but furniture retailers aren’t waiting for the official festivities to begin. Some of our favorite brands are already rolling out discounts on living room furniture, bedroom sets, and statement pieces that have absolutely no business being in our shopping cart but somehow end up there anyway. Considering how rapidly foundational pieces like a new sofa, bed frame, or dresser can gobble up a decorating budget, we’re certainly not complaining.

Of course, not every early November sale is technically a Black Friday sale. Some brands are soft launching their holiday shopping season while others are tempting us with fall clearance events and limited-time promotions. Either way, there is an abundance of furniture deals worth shopping well before November 27. We’ve rounded up early Black Friday furniture deals from 14 retailers that should be on your home decor radar, including AD-tested favorites, designer collaborations, and plenty of pieces that might finally convince you to patch that room you’ve been meaning to refresh.

According to recent reports, A good night’s sleep is an invaluable investment, but that doesn't mean you have to pay full price for it. Saatva is presently offering up to $625 off orders, giving you a head start on upgrading your sleep set up if a luxurious mattress is on your wishlist. Note: You need a mattress in your cart for the discount to apply. The Loom & Leaf is particularly attractive for memory foam devotees, which contributor Bailey Berg previously described as the “most breathable, comfortable mattress” she’d ever tried. And if a bedroom overhaul is in the cards, Saatva’s upholstered Halle storage platform bed offers a discreet place to stash extra bedding totally out of sight.

A little coastal influence can go a long way, even if the nearest beach is blanketed in snow during the off-season. Serena & Lily is currently hosting The Sale of the Year, with up to 40% off furniture, mirrors, and lighting, plus discounts across nearly every other product category. It’s a chance to bring the brand’s breezy, tailored aesthetic home in time for the holidays. We’re particularly fond of its outdoor lineup, including the Pacifica Sofa, which AD contributor Blake Bakkila put to the test for more than three years at her Newport Beach home. Despite its exposure to coastal moisture, she reported no fading, warping, or damage, and gave the sofa an overall A rating. For an indoor refresh, the Carter counter stool brings the brand’s signature natural texture into the kitchen.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a reason Wayfair is a go-to destination when a room needs furnishing without a designer-size budget. The retailer’s Holiday Flash Sale is underway, with discounts of up to 70% sitewide. Its family of brands includes AllModern, a favorite for contemporary silhouettes at relatively approachable prices. AD contributor Elise Portale tested the AllModern Breanna chaise sectional, praising its soft upholstery. “At the end of the day, the best way I can describe it is ‘luxurious,’” she said. Take your living room refresh a step further with a ladder bookcase from Madison Park, or get a head start on decking the halls with festive finds at wallet-friendly prices.

For those with a penchant for clean-lined furniture, Article’s vast catalog of ready-to-ship mid-century-inspired pieces is a treasure trove. A sale section filled with last-chance pieces priced at up to 40% off only sweetens the deal. Don’t sleep on the Tessu bed frame, either, especially if you’re looking to soften up your bedroom with its low profile and ivory wool boucle upholstery.

In a recent development, A design classic rarely comes cheap, which makes Design Within Reach’s current Herman Miller promotion particularly noteworthy. Right now, you can score 20% off the brand’s iconic modern desk chairs and 25% off task and gaming chairs. For a home office that deserves a little more consideration than the average desk-and-chair combination, look to the Eames Soft Pad Management Chair or George Nelson’s Swag Leg Desk. Think of this as your sign to incorporate a little bit of legendary mid-century design into your workday for a fraction of the price. And don’t overlook Herman Miller’s lighting, tables, and home decor pieces, which are also included in this rare sale.

Industry observers note that crate & Barrel’s designer collaborations are reason enough to redecorate, but throw in a 30% off Accent Furniture Sale and deeply discounted clearance finds, and the temptation is harder to resist. We’ve been drawn to the collection created by actor Laura Harrier and interior designer Tiffany Howell, which debuted in April and pairs richly layered materials and vintage influences to contemporary furniture. Their Siren queen bed is at the moment 33% off, or you can snag Jake Arnold’s Sculptural Metal Accent Chair for 20% off, among other hidden gems.

Joybird’s extensive upholstery catalog and seemingly endless configuration options make up for every sad millennial-gray starter sofa that’s seen one move too many. The brand’s early Black Friday sale offers up to 45% off select furniture, including its distinctive, customizable seating. AD senior entertainment editor Rachel Wallace chose the Sebastian sofa in a vibrant chartreuse velvet and was won over by its rounded silhouette and generous proportions. “This is by far the most supreme nap sofa I have ever experienced,” she said. The Sebastian is just one of many seating options worth considering, along with the Amelia grand swivel chair, a cozy contender for reading nooks and movie nights.

In a recent development, amazon’s furniture selection can require some digging, but there are worthwhile finds among the seemingly endless listings, particularly for bedroom basics. Allewie is among our favorite furniture brands on Amazon, and early deals on its already affordable pieces can save you up to 33%. The brand’s lift-up hydraulic storage bed frame is an especially practical pick for bedrooms short on closet space, offering concealed storage beneath the mattress. “I think the best part of the frame is that it takes up a good amount of space without being excessive, allowing for a good variety of bedroom setup,” states contributor Will Porter, who tested the bed frame at home. The brand’s black oak wooden bed frame takes a more understated approach with a sleek, modern headboard and footboard, but don’t stop there. Amazon has plenty of discounted furniture for the rest of your home, too.

It has been revealed that shea McGee has the magic touch for making spaces feel collected and curated, and McGee & Co.’s furniture reflects the designer’s signature sensibility. The brand’s current sale features up to 70% off select pieces, with substantial reductions on dining chairs, end tables, nightstands, and bedroom furniture. The Beacon nightstand is 40% off, and the Gilmore canopy bed, a modern minimalist’s dream, is marked down to its lowest price ever. These contemporary heirlooms are more likely to be passed down from one generation to the next than they are to go out of style, so these prices are practically a steal.

West Elm is hosting The Fall Sale, offering up to 60% off plus an extra 20% off select styles. The brand’s midcentury-inspired dressers and nightstands are perennial favorites, but we’re particularly interested in the Shelter Sleeper sofa for anyone expecting out-of-town guests this holiday season. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert tested the queen-size version in dark olive performance velvet and called it “the softest, cushiest couch in my house.” Another standout from the sale is the midcentury five-drawer dresser, a handsome storage solution narrow enough for smaller bedrooms and cozy apartments. Equally impressive deals can be found on accent chairs, dining tables, and some of the brand’s bestsellers.

According to recent reports, pottery Barn’s extensive selection of living room, dining room, and bedroom furniture has earned it a reputation as a one-stop shop for furnishing an entire space. Its current Fall Sale includes up to 70% of select furniture, with additional discounts on certain styles. The brand is known for its comfortable, traditional seating, including the York Slope Arm Deep Seat Slipcovered Side Sleeper, at the moment 20% off. Contributor Kate McGregor tested the sofa and praised its plush cushions, washable slipcover, and easy-to-use sleeper mechanism. “This is one of the most comfortable sofas I’ve had the pleasure of sitting on,” she wrote. If your living room doubles as your guest room, this is one deal you won’t want to skip.

It’s rare that a sofa is so versatile that it can adapt to a upcoming apartment, growing household, or an entirely different floor blueprint, but not at Burrow. The direct-to-consumer furniture brand is already hosting a Black Friday Preview with up to 40% off. Its modular seating arrives in manageable sections that can be easily rearranged or expanded as your needs change. Contributor David Kaufman tested the Range three-piece open sectional lounger, which he described as a “crowd-pleaser in the house.” The Nomad leather sofa with ottoman is equally tempting, especially if a more tailored take is more your speed.

In a recent development, perusing Nickey Kehoe’s sale section is akin to sifting through buried treasure. The Los Angeles design studio and retailer is known for furniture that feels thoughtful, rich with character, and difficult to pin to any one decorating era. Its Last Chance section offers up to 30% off distinctive pieces like the architectural Iron Canopy Bed and the Community Harvest Bench. Both have the kind of lived-in appeal that makes a room look as though it’s been furnished gradually, with pieces collected over time.

Recent findings suggest that if your home office has been getting by with a less-than-ideal setup, Haworth’s current sale is a good reason to treat yourself. The office furniture specialist is right now offering 25% off select performance seating, desks, gaming furniture, lighting, and accessories, with ergonomic favorites like the Fern, Zody, and Soji chairs among its most popular pieces. But, the sale extends beyond seating. The Market Wire Frame Desk offers an industrial-leaning alternative to a conventional writing table, and the Elements Laminate Flare Leg Desk brings a cleaner, more minimalist silhouette to the workspace. Considering how much time we spend at our desks, a workspace that looks as good as it works hardly seems like an unreasonable indulgence.

The 6 Best Compression Boots to Support Muscle Recovery, Tested by Fitness Editors

📅 31 Oct 2022 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3214 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MY RECOVERY ROUTINE has included quality time in my compression boots for a few years now.
  • It has been revealed that while several brands offer compression boots for workout recovery, it's clear to us that Hyperice and Therabody reign supreme.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Compression boots were initially designed to treat various medical conditions related to poor circulation and fluid retention," explains Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MY RECOVERY ROUTINE has included quality time in my compression boots for a few years now. For a lot of guys (myself included) self care is not a strong suit. For many years I went hard until the wheels came off, and eventually I learned I could increase my lower-body blood flow, and thus recover quicker, by using a foam roller. But incorporating compression boots into my post-run regime (even if it is a slightly different recovery stimulus) has forced me to take time for myself and also allowed me to enjoy watching some sports while doing the "right thing" for my body.

It has been revealed that while several brands offer compression boots for workout recovery, it's clear to us that Hyperice and Therabody reign supreme. Since our initial 2021 review of Therabody's compression boots, the brand has introduced an innovative and affordable wireless iteration known as the JetBoots Prime. On the Hyperice front, a compact solution called the Normatec Go is an uber-portable compression boot system that targets the calves and allows for easy on-the-go recovery. And most recently it released the Normatec Elites, which have elevated the game with a wireless design.

Recent findings suggest that "Compression boots were initially designed to treat various medical conditions related to poor circulation and fluid retention," explains Dr. Renato Sanchez, PT, DPT, C.S.C.S. Over the last few years, compression therapy has gained popularity in the fitness industry as a muscle recovery tool—especially after the previous popularity of percussion massage guns.

It has been revealed that for those who may have doubts regarding how effective compression boots really are in terms of muscle recovery, we understand your concerns. Let's clarify that there is still a significant shortage of scientific research supporting claims about the effectiveness of compression boots in expediting or enhancing the recovery process. (Brands might tell you otherwise, but we only go by the independent studies.) Instead, we can only tell you how we've felt after using them firsthand.

"Compression boots do have value," indicates MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. "The end result is definitely relaxing—thus allowing my nervous system to down regulate. That down regulation has recovery value.".

To simplify the process of choosing from the massive range of options, we've put together a guide to buying compression boots for various individuals. Up next, you'll find our thoroughly tested and vetted backing of the six best compression boots, suitable for every workout routine and budget.

From the moment that the Normatec Elites arrive at your door, fully charged and ready to help you recover within moments, you know that you've made the right choice in compression boot. Normatec has been at the forefront of compression boot technology since it rolled out in 1998, and has only got better since it was acquired by recovery brand Hyperice in 2020.

I am a fan of how simple it is to get started, just zip your legs into the sleeves and select the compression level and desired treatment time. The attachments begin to inflate in sequence, starting with your feet and moving upwards. For the amount of relief they provide, the sleeves are fairly light, but you can't really move around much one you are zipped up.

According to recent reports, there are no external cords necessary, which is nice. The package comes with a charger that can be used to charge both attachments at the same time. It also comes with a travel bag that you can use to pack the attachments if you want to take them on any trips.

Industry observers note that putting these on after an intense run or leg workout has become a ritual, and I struggle to think of any complaints I have with this unit. They are sleek looking, simple to use, and really help elevate your recovery time at home (or on the go).Read More: Normatec Elite Review.

We were fans of the Therabody JetBoots when they first released, with a streamlined design eliminating cords and separate controllers. Now the JetBoots Prime from Therabody bring those same benefits we enjoyed for a few hundred dollars less. So we're not going to complain.

These boots are easy to move around the home, so you can throw them on anywhere to enjoy the 20-100 mmHg pressure handsfree. These boots have accompanied us on the couch, in bed, and even inside an airport lounge. It's an untethered experience that's super convenient, whether you're newly introduced to compression boots or not. Put 'em on, press the buttons on one leg (they're auto-paired, which we found even more convenient), and the air-massage begins.There is also something nice about being limited to four time intervals (20 minutes, 40 minutes, 60 minutes, continuous) and four pressure levels (25, 50, 75, 100 mmHg). Sometimes minimizing the options makes everything a little more straight forward. This is all managed with the simple control panel on the Primes that's conveniently designed into one of the boots. If you're not wanting to splurge for the Pro system, these are the boots for you.

Perhaps the coolest design of compression boots yet, our editors found the portable Normatec Go boots easy to transport and simple to use. The one downside is that they only cover the calves, so it's not ideal for those looking to tackle hamstring and quad soreness and recovery. But, if you're someone whose calves cry out following a workout and are looking to dip your toes in the world of compression boots without making too significant of an investment, these are an excellent choice.

These boots don't sacrifice on performance even though they're smaller. We found that the Go especially shines following a long run or full day of walking. "I've had to travel for a few races and these sleeves are a great recovery tool that don't take up an entire piece of luggage," claims Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM.

Plus, it can be functional to get the compression your calves need without being stuck in a lying position on the couch. The Go's offer a bit more mobility to play video games or work from a laptop–we've even used a pair on an airplane.

Read More: Hyperice Normatec Go Review.

Recent findings suggest that for those in search of a full spa experience for their legs, the PRO Plus system from Therabody aims to give it to you, daring to integrate vibration and red light therapy into its compression boots. Like other models on this list, they show up at your door fully charged. Even with all the additional technology, these boots are surprisingly lightweight, and don't feel too bulky on the legs.

Sources indicate that the red light therapy isn't a game-changer (although it does make for a cool selling point). But the vibration is a nice addition to the treatment, and while the actual recovery benefits from it may be negligible, it is pleasant. We also like that the Pros can be programmed with your favorite preset settings, so they're locked and loaded whenever you're ready to get a session in.

They also come with two special preset programs you can't get on the Prime or the original JetBoots: Isolation and Interval mode. From there, the customization gets more intense. We're talking adjustable pressure time, hold time, and pressure range that provide the opportunity to work your muscles the best way you see fit at any given moment.

Normatec's Full Body system is practical than most other full-body systems out there. Reason being, this version covers the areas people are more likely to be sore in, like the hips and legs, as well as the arms. Hyperice's attachments here are just better, and the straps make them fairly simple to put on by yourself. The only pain point is if you want to use both arm attachments, you'll likely need someone to help you strap in.

The ability to treat your hips and arms is a big win for anyone looking for a more well-rounded solution. And while compression to this extent doesn't guarantee muscle recovery, a half hour treatment will definitely help you relax after an intense session or even just rough day at the office. (Just note that the arms are pretty restrictive to don; don't expect to type emails comfortably while treating your biceps and triceps.).

Sources indicate that the Normatec 3.0 control unit can plug into two attachments at a time, so it is up to you whether you want to treat both legs, two arms, or any other combination of two. For a true full body treatment, you can alternate between sides after your first session is complete.

The Hyperboots were first revealed at the 2024 Paris Olympics and were used by athletes like LeBron James during the games, along with a vest that also featured similar technology. After the reveal, the MH team was excited to get our hands on these, and when we did this summer, we weren’t disappointed.

The Hyperboots, which look more like high-tech, high-top sneakers than boots, show up in a sleek black box emblazoned with the logos for Hyperice and Nike like any other pair of footwear. The boots themselves have a great aesthetic, looking cool enough to even wear on the streets of New York. In order to be used, they are charged with a standard USB-C cable (a welcome sight as opposed to other devices that try to create proprietary chargers).

Industry observers note that let's be clear though, these Hyperboots aren't true compression boots, so you may not get all of the benefits we mentioned above. But you do get a piece of gear that is unique an innovative with sequential air compression combined with targeted heat, which makes it a solid warmup device, as well as a solid late night recovery option, when you want to hit errands as you treat.

Sources indicate that once you’re strapped into the shoes, there are three compression settings, going up to 210 mmHg—more than any other device in this guide. There are also three heat settings going up to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, which is more than you need. “Nike definitely got things right from a tech perspective,” notes MH Fitness Director, Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. who got an early pair sent. “The compression and heat is great, especially around the heel. I only wish I was feeling the compression the same on my entire foot.”.

Industry observers note that the consensus on the Hyperboots is that they are an impressive piece of technology that bring relief to a part of our body that takes a lot of punishment, especially if you are training hard. And while the cost is a little high, these stylish sneakers do help alleviate aches, making them a valid purchase if you have the means. Hyperice’s Normatec Elites have become a regular part of my recovery routine, and I could see the Hyperboots becoming one, too.

The unit of measure that you will see when describing the pressure that these compression boots give is millimeters of mercury (or mmHg). The minimum amount you will commonly see is 20 mmHg, which is a similar amount of pressure that you would get from your standard compression sock, with it going up from there. The ability to adjust compression intensity is essential to accommodate varying recovery needs and your own preferences.

Some products offer more adjustability and levels of compression than others, allowing you to fine-tune your experience to the exact compression you're looking for. Look for boots that offer as much adjustability as possible, with no less than four compression levels.

Consider the convenience of putting on and taking off the compression boots. Look for user-friendly designs with simple controls or automated features that make using and operating the boots—from start to finish—simple and accessible. Wireless capabilities have become a little more prevalent, and obviously offer the simplest and most portable option—though they often come with a heftier price tag.

If you initiative to use the boots at home or while traveling, consider portability and storage options. Compact designs (such as the Normatec Go) or accompanying carrying cases can make transportation and storage more convenient. And again, the wireless design is key for portability and on-the-go use.

For battery-operated compression boots, evaluate the battery life and charging time. Longer battery life ensures uninterrupted use during recovery sessions, while quick charging capabilities reduce downtime between uses. We recommend looking for a battery life of three hours or more for an optimal experience. While you won't (read: should not) use your boots for three hours in a single session, a long battery life ensures you have to charge them after every session.

Industry observers note that explore any extra features or functionalities offered by the compression boots, such as massage modes, heat therapy, or integration with mobile apps for personalized recovery programs. The Hyperice products on this list feature connectivity with the brand's app, while the Therabody app features Bluetooth connectivity that learns from your use and integrates into Apple Health and Google Fit. Remember, though, that what you're chasing with compression boots should be quality compression. Brands love blending in other traits (red-light therapy, etc.), but don't pay extra for these.

In a recent development, research the reputation of the brand and read reviews from other owners to gauge the effectiveness and reliability of the compression boots. Many brands provide compression boots for post-workout recovery, but our testing has revealed Therabody and Hyperice as the most trusted. Since our initial evaluation in 2021, we have been continuously impressed by the reliability and quality of these two brands.

Being the Fitness and Reviews Editor of Men's Health means I get my hands on every piece of upcoming recovery gear that releases, sometimes before it releases. To build this guide to the best compression boots, I compared the best-selling boots on the market with overlooked classics and newly released options.

Along with Men's Health fitness editors and experts including Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, we invested countless hours to put all major compression boot brands to the test by evaluating each model's comfort, fit, ease of use, value, and overall performance. We also sought expertise from physical therapists Renato Sanchez, PT, DPT, C.S.C.S. of Bespoke Treatments San Diego and Dan Giordano, PT, DPT, C.S.C.S. of Bespoke Treatments NYC to understand the role compression can play in recovery and rehabilitation.

Compression boots work by using air pressure to control the blood circulation in your legs.

Recent findings suggest that "As each chamber in the boots fills with air and compresses more tightly, it prevents a large amount of blood from circulating through that part of your body," says Samuel. "So when the boots tighten around your feet first and then your calves, your blood flow to those areas is limited. As this compression continues around your entire leg, you’re left with even more limited blood flow. But just a moment after all that, the chambers methodically deflate, permitting blood to travel first into your thighs, then down through your lower legs, then into your feet.".

The theory behind this practice is the onrush of blood will help bring nutrients to help your legs recover efficiently, but this has not been proven for fact.

Sources indicate that "There is conflicting evidence that compression devices aid in long term muscle recovery from delayed onset muscle soreness," according to Dr. Sanchez. "However, there has been research that suggests short term relief from exercise induced muscle damage.".

Despite the lack of proof, the gentle squeezing of the leg muscles can feel relaxing—even massage-like at times.

To ensure your blood circulation doesn't get cut off Therabody and Hyperice have capped its devices to only reach specific amounts of pressure (measured in mmHG). So as long as you properly place the boots on your legs and use them for the time settings given, your risk of injury is low. Just make sure if you're fresh to using compression boots you start with the lowest setting first with short periods of time. Then, as you get more comfortable with using your compression boots, you can play with the higher mmHG levels and time settings.

According to recent reports, buying a pair of compression boots is no small investment, which is why we took the time to vet the most trustworthy products above. Painting in broad brushstrokes, compression boots are largely expensive because you're bringing high-level compression therapy tech into to the comfort of your own home.

So with the price points you see with Hyperice and Therabody, you have to consider the amount of research and development needed to help advanced the compression boots while still being easy to use. Features like simple control panels, built-in internal pumps, preset programs, and compression targeting are several examples of tech that's been improved upon in the last few years.

Recent findings suggest that second to consider is portability, as brands have been able to condense the size to make them relatively easy to move around the house and travel with. Last is safety, as brands have to make sure the compression boots operate within a specific boundary to ensure you receive a tightening effect on your muscles without going too far and potentially causing injury.

In a recent development, compression boots can be used every day, according to Dr. Giordano. Especially for intense exercisers.

It has been revealed that aim to wait a few hours after any workout, says Samuel, to get the most out of your compression boots. "Removing inflammation too soon after a workout doesn't give your body a chance to adapt to the training stimulus you just created," says Samuel. "Think of compression boots as an ideal way to end a tough training day, instead of using them immediately after a run or workout.".

Sources indicate that there's another use for them, too. "They are commonly used after intense exercise, but can also be used prior to exercise as part of a warm up routine," claims Dr. Sanchez. "I suggest using them for 10-15 minutes pre exercise.".

Keep in mind: It’s important to first discuss with a healthcare professional to determine if compression boots are right for you.

When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

Breaking: BYD and Geely approached FIA about a 12th F1 team, states Ben Sulayem

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1023 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed.
  • In a recent development, but there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal.
  • “One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem remarked of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the New Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio.

In a recent development, but there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither company has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.

“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem remarked of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.

He remarked he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a newly introduced one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the company to come back with a “serious proposal” that indicates the project can work.

He also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.

Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

Sources indicate that this isn’t newly introduced for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry, either by buying a team or building one from scratch.

In April, executive vice president Stella Li noted BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”.

Altavilla said BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.

Geely is the new name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.

The last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.

In a recent development, here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.

The FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali claims F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.

So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.

We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.

Industry observers note that they look for visibility/recognition on the world stage, regardless EVs. And in some (primitive) markets they market themselves as hybrids automakers, not as EV automakers.

They will make a hybrid power unit (which they already make anyway) to comply with the backward F1 regulations.

Industry observers note that but Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.

A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.

Sources indicate that if you’re following how fast EV tech is moving, from BYD’s batteries to F1’s hybrid power units, you can put some of that tech to work at home: pairing an EV with rooftop solar can cut your driving costs to nearly zero. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes.
  • After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its newly introduced ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.
  • The Chinese automaker released a latest integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.

After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its newly introduced ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.

The Chinese automaker released a latest integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.

In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.

The new charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

The latest robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.

By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD said the latest tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.

Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.

A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez).

Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the new charging tech in action.

In a recent development, the integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.

Industry observers note that if they could tie this into a smart summon type of capability, where the vehicle communicates with the charger and moves the vehicle into the proper location for charging and then moves to a parking spot once charging is complete. Rental car fleets would benefit and so would those in shopping centers. There are so many possibilities and this looks far more mature that the old snake charging Tesla demoed.

BYD has over 16 years of experience in the solar industry with a portfolio that includes solar cells, modules, and systems.

Its solar division, BYD Solar, does business in over 100 countries and regions. By using solar power, BYD noted, the SCC system can operate independently off-the-grid.

According to recent reports, the new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company plans to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that editor’s Note: When I originally reported this article in 2014, a pound of ground beef cost roughly $3.50.
  • Sources indicate that and, if you can spring for grass-fed beef, there’s been more recent published research to show that it might be healthier for you than the grain-fed variety.
  • While eating healthier is great, doing so has to taste amazing too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that editor’s Note: When I originally reported this article in 2014, a pound of ground beef cost roughly $3.50. Now that same amount of protein costs you $6.75. But nothing about buying beef wholesale has changed: You will still save more money over time if you purchase an eighth, a quarter, a half, or even a whole cow given you have the upfront cash and deep freezer space to store it all. (A quarter of a cow from the same farm I purchased mine now costs $1,100, in case you were wondering.).

Sources indicate that and, if you can spring for grass-fed beef, there’s been more recent published research to show that it might be healthier for you than the grain-fed variety. In 2022, South Korean researchers found that grass-fed beef contained a healthier fatty acid profile than grain-fed beef. Same goes for a 2026 study published in the Journal of Animal Science.

While eating healthier is great, doing so has to taste amazing too. Luckily that hasn’t changed about grass-fed beef either.

THE COW I ate was born in rural Pennsylvania. Cathy Pomanti, the owner of Sugar Hill Farm, midwifed my calf into the world. Pomanti raises grass-fed organic Scottish Highland Cows, a shaggy breed yielding meat that’s among the tastiest on the planet. On one farm visit, my fiancee saw a highlander, went quiet, and then noted, “I don’t want to eat them. I want to hug them.” But I was hungry for a cow to call my own.

In a recent development, as a pleasure-seeking meat eater, disappointed by grain-fed supermarket beef. Rib eyes require a slick of steak sauce to taste meaty. Ground beef has a tacky, greasy consistency. Tenderloin, even with tender care, always leaves me underwhelmed. So I decided to stop complaining about mass-market beef and find a rancher. I wanted to know my cattle producer. I wanted to know my cow.

Industry observers note that my cow never had a name; Pomanti can’t bring herself to name cows headed for slaughter. But he did have a good life. My cow spent his first 10 months growing strong on his mother’s milk, sticking close by her side. Then Pomanti separated my cow and his mother into different pens. My cow bawled. His mother mooed. It was for the best. Once Mom stopped producing milk, the two were reunited, but my cow now preferred delicious, nutritious grass.

Over the next year and a half, my cow grew an impressive coat of thick, coarse hair. Because he wouldn’t be subjected to the diseases and indignities of the industrial feedlot, he didn’t need antibiotics or growth hormones. Those substances wouldn’t end up in me or my fiancée, either.

Recent findings suggest that last October, my cow was loaded onto a truck and taken to Rising Spring Meat Tech giant, an organic butcher outside State College, Pennsylvania. There he was held in a pen, calm and comfortable, until he was humanely shot in the head. The carcass was then halved and hung in a cooler to dry-age, a process that helps tenderize the meat, for about 14 days. Next my cow was cut into pieces, vacuum-sealed, and delivered to Pomanti.

She summoned me for the handoff. Out of her massive freezer units she pulled bags bursting with marrow bones, globular ground beef portions, and a tenderloin the size of Popeye’s forearm. I drove the box of beef back home that day, dreaming of meals to come, under a sky with clouds that looked like heifers.

According to recent reports, AS A TYPICAL American, you ate a hefty 51 pounds of beef last year, the USDA notes. That’s roughly the equivalent of 65 T-bones or 204 quarter-pound burger patties.

The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association notes that less than 1 percent of beef sold at retail is labeled as grass-fed. During the “finishing,” the animal begins to lay down more fat in relation to muscle and bone growth, says Cindy Daley, Ph.D., who studies beef at California State University.

It has been revealed that until the 1950s, ranchers finished cattle exclusively on grass. But industrial producers realized that grain feeding improved fat marbling while cutting the days until slaughter. After decades of eating the stuff, we now prefer fattier beef. But at the same time, our rates of diseases linked to inflammation rose.

Could grain-fed cows and inflammation be connected? A 2011 Irish study found that people who replaced their regular red meat with three weekly servings of grass-fed red meat for a month improved their inflammation-fighting omega-3 fatty acid profiles by 37 percent over those of people who ate the same amount of grain-finished red meat.

Though the diet studies are too small to be conclusive, a 2010 research review led by Daley found that grass-fed beef outclassed grain-fed nutritionally, with triple the immune-boosting vitamin E, up to five times the heart-healthy omega-3 fatty acids, and seven times the antioxidant carotenoids.

If grass-fed beef was going to treat me better, I needed to return the favor. So I began contacting chefs. The recipes that follow taught me key kitchen skills, but they also taught me something deeper: If you know your beef, you love it even more.

Sources indicate that THERE’S A CERTAIN comfort in dissociating yourself from the animal you’re eating for dinner. If you don’t think about where on the cow’s body the meat comes from, you don’t have to contemplate the death and dismemberment involved in its trip to your plate. The oxtail, however, made a very specific statement about its origins. It came to me in three pieces, which, because of my morbid curios- ity, I arranged to reconstruct the entire appendage. I imagined my cow using it to swat flies. It wasn’t simply a meal. It was a sacrifice.

Recent findings suggest that alice Waters, executive chef of Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, and founder of the Edible Schoolyard Project, recommends cooking oxtail in a classic braise. “With grain-fed beef, you’re tasting a richness and tenderness, but it’s not the real flavor,” Waters states. “It’s like cooking vegetables with a lot of butter: You can’t taste the vegetables.” Her technique, inspired by a recipe from Zuni Café in San Francisco, matches the beautiful beefiness of the rustic cut while also turning it fork-tender.

Bonus: You can apply the same braising technique to other tough bone-in cuts your purveyor may pass along, such as shanks or short ribs.

2 lb grass-fed oxtails1 Tbsp Kosher salt4 cups beef stock2 Tbsp olive oil1 ¾ cups red wine2 bay leaves1 small head garlic, halved crosswise1 sprig thyme3 black peppercorns1 large carrot, peeled and roughly chopped3 celery stalks, roughly chopped1 medium yellow onion, quartered1 cup drained canned tomatoes, roughly chopped.

1. For the best flavor, salt the oxtails two days before cooking.

2. Trim the oxtails of excess fat. In a medium saucepan, cook the stock over medium heat until reduced by half, about 30 minutes.

3. In a skillet, heat the oil on medium. Pat the oxtails dry and brown them, 3 to 4 minutes. Set aside. Wipe the skillet, add the wine, stir, and cook it down by half, about 5 minutes. Add the stock.

Industry observers note that 4. Preheat the oven to 300°F. In a roasting pan, add the remaining ingredients; add stock to cover by a third. Simmer on medium low. Cover.

According to recent reports, 5. Place the pan in the oven and cook 3 to 4 hours. Then crack the lid and cook until the meat is very tender, another 20 to 30 minutes. Serve oxtails with sauce. Makes 8 servings.

Recent findings suggest that I NEEDED TO do something special with the most prestigious cut of my cow: the 14-pound standing rib roast. The meal should be special but also very simple, indicates Donald Link, owner and executive chef of Cochon and Butcher in New Orleans. Anything too fussy would only detract from its intense, glorious beefiness.

Recent findings suggest that for maximum flavor, you want to cook this behemoth roast only to medium rare, Link told me. Because the cut is so large, the preparation and resting stages are critical. If the meat is too cold before it enters the oven, it’ll be raw in the center when it exits. If you carve into it immediately after cooking, you’ll lose a reservoir of delicious juices. Patience is paramount.

And the rewards are well worth the wait: “Good grass-fed beef tastes cleaner. You don’t have that heavy feeling in your gut after you eat it,” Link says. I heard similar accolades from the friends and family members I invited over to dinner. In fact, most people said the steaks, liver, or carne asada I’d served them tasted “like beefier beef” and “less greasy.” One guest who tasted the rib roast said she woke up the morning after our dinner fantasizing about the beef from the night before.

1 grass-fed beef rib roast (14 lb)Olive oil.

Recent findings suggest that 1. To promote even doneness, remove the roast from the refrigerator 2 hours before cooking.

2. Place the roast on a wire rack set on a baking sheet. The last 30 minutes prior to cooking, place a fan in front of the meat to dry excess moisture and foster caramelization.

Industry observers note that 3. Preheat the oven to 450°F. Lightly rub the roast on all sides with olive oil and then liberally coat it with salt and freshly ground pepper. Set it back on the wire rack atop the baking sheet and place it in the oven.

Sources indicate that 4. Cook until well browned on the outside, about 20 minutes. Lower the heat to 275°F and continue to cook until a digital thermometer inserted into the center of the roast reads 140°F, about 2 hours. Remove the roast and let it rest until it’s almost at room temperature, about 45 minutes.

5. Serve with roasted potatoes and a simple salad. Makes 20 to 25 servings.

OF THE 51 pounds of cow you ate last year, about half was ground. Here’s a scary fact: U.S. ground beef is not easily traced and may not even be from the United States, a 2013 review in Meat Science reveals. All the more reason to buddy up to a rancher.

You can make a grass-fed beef burger (I did), but you’d be depriving your tastebuds if you didn’t venture beyond familiar ground. “Grass-fed beef is very lean by nature. Grinding beef for burgers involves adding fat, and if you’re using grass-fed, you lose something,” says Sang Yoon, executive chef of Father’s Office and Lukshon in L.A. That something, he says, is the herbaceous flavor imparted by the cow’s diet. Make larb instead, Yoon says. This Southeast Asian dish packs a barrage of fresh herbs to flatter grass-fed beef.

1 Tbsp uncooked jasmine rice6 Tbsp peanut oil12 oz grass-fed ground beef1 shallot, minced2 garlic cloves, sliced2 fresh Thai chiles, thinly sliced1 Tbsp palm sugar2 Tbsp fish sauce¼ cup lime juice1 head cabbage, leaves separated½ cilantro leaves½ mint leaves½ Thai basil leaves4 scallions, sliced.

1. In a small pan on medium heat, toast the rice, stirring often. Cool and grind the rice to a fine powder in a clean coffee or spice grinder.

2. In a wok or massive cast-iron skillet, heat the oil on medium high until it shimmers. Add the beef; cook, stirring occasionally, until it begins to brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Add the shallot, garlic, chiles, palm sugar, and fish sauce.

3. Remove from the heat and add the lime juice and rice powder. Stir well and season with salt.

4. Let the mixture cool slightly before serving. Spoon the mixture into individual cabbage cups and garnish with herbs and scallions. Makes 6 to 8 servings.

It has been revealed that MARC FORGIONE, OWNER and executive chef of Restaurant Marc Forgione in Fresh York City, told me I should start by not cooking the beef at all. “The best way to experience grass-fed beef, because it’s so lean, is to eat it raw,” says Forgione.

When I asked him if it was dangerous to eat DIY steak tartare, Forgione told me that as long as the beef is high in quality and its temperature never rises above 40°F for longer than 40 minutes, your risk of illness will be very low, he claims. And Pomanti, for her part, says bacterial contamination among her cattle is vir- tually nonexistent. (It pays to know your source.).

According to recent reports, so I sharpened my knives for a rare opportunity. The result was a luscious tartare that topped variations I’ve tasted at the country’s top steakhouses.

1 Tbsp minced onion1 Tbsp minced cornichons1 tsp minced parsley2 anchovies, minced½ Tbsp Dijon mustard2 or 3 dashes Tabasco sauce2 tsp Worcestershire sauce½ cup, plus 2 Tbsp olive oil1 lb grass-fed beef tenderloinWarm toast.

In a recent development, 1. In a small bowl, mix the onion, parsley, cornichons, and anchovies. Reserve.

Recent findings suggest that 2. In a blender or food processor, add the mustard, Tabasco, Worcestershire, and 2 Tbsp olive oil. Puree, gradually adding the remaining olive oil until emulsified. Reserve.

3. Place the tenderloin in the freezer for about 5 minutes for easier cutting. Then, working rapidly, slice it into ¼-inch-thick pieces.

In a recent development, 4. In a medium serving bowl, combine the meat with the reserved ingredients. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Mix well.

Industry observers note that 5. Chill in the fridge for 10 minutes before serving atop warm toast. Makes 8 servings as an appetizer.

WHEN MY TOUR of the special cuts was complete, I dug for the last of the T-bones that were stashed aside the cow’s heart (yes, the heart) in the freezer. Steaks were the first cuts I cooked, and I still craved them. Naomi Pomeroy, the executive chef of Beast in Portland, Oregon, had taught me to sear them to a juicy medium rare. She’s a pro; she cooks grass-fed beef exclusively.

I preheated my oven to 350°F and placed a cast-iron skillet over medium heat. I cranked some freshly ground black pepper and scattered kosher salt over each side of the steak. Then I added a good knob of butter to the skillet, allowed it to melt, and followed it with the steak and a few sprigs of parsley and thyme. I listened for the sizzling to subside, awaiting the aroma of a baseball field on a hot summer day. Those signs told me it was time to flip the meat and then slide it into the oven, skillet and all. There it basked for five minutes until the interior temperature reached 122°F. Out of the oven it came. I then basted it reverently with the rest of the melted butter, tented some aluminum foil over the skillet, and let it rest for what seemed like an eternity. Okay, five minutes. And then I savored every last juicy, earthy, hearty, powerful, tender bite. The celebration of my cow was complete.

Yes, grass-fed beef costs more money than the grain-finished variety, but you’re making that investment to enjoy superior meat that is less fatty, more nutrient-dense, better for your body, and certainly better on the palate.

And if you purchase your grass-fed beef in bulk, so much the better. It can be less expensive than grass-fed cuts you’d find in the store, for one thing. There’s also something deeply comfort- ing about possessing a large amount of premium meat. (Zombie apocalypse be damned!) But because you know the life of your cow, and the rancher who raised that animal, you also want to honor that cow in death. It’s not just dinner. It’s your duty.

You can have a heart—and cook one, too.

Perps and Swaps: How to Trade the News on Decrypt

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Decrypt

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that readers have traditionally learned about markets in one place and traded them in another.
  • Decrypt set out to close that gap in September 2026, when it announced The Information Exchange: a network that brings together news, data, market prices, probabilities and the ability to trade, around the subjects readers follow.
  • The Information Exchange sees Decrypt delivering both the reporting and the market infrastructure that links information to trading, while the Solana blockchain provides the network on which trades settle, including token swaps and perpetual futures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that readers have traditionally learned about markets in one place and traded them in another. A story about Bitcoin, a public tech giant or a commodity might shape a view, but acting on it meant opening an exchange or a trading app and starting over.

Decrypt set out to close that gap in September 2026, when it announced The Information Exchange: a network that brings together news, data, market prices, probabilities and the ability to trade, around the subjects readers follow.

The Information Exchange sees Decrypt delivering both the reporting and the market infrastructure that links information to trading, while the Solana blockchain provides the network on which trades settle, including token swaps and perpetual futures.

This guide explains what each one is and how to trade it on Decrypt.

Everything on The Information Exchange runs through a Decrypt Money Account, which rolled out on Solana in October 2026.

A Money Account holds one balance that funds every product on Decrypt: swaps, perpetual futures and prediction markets.The account is self-custodial, meaning Decrypt does not hold users' private keys and cannot act on their behalf. It is designed to work without seed phrases, and network fees are covered, so users don't need to hold SOL, Solana's native token, to pay for transactions.

Recent findings suggest that in November 2026, Decrypt added confidential transfers, using Solana Privacy Rings from infrastructure firm Helius. Consumers can send funds without the amounts appearing on Solana's public ledger, and can switch the feature on by selecting "Enable" on the Private Balance panel of the Portfolio page. As of November 2026, privacy applies to transfers only, not to swaps or prediction market positions.

Solana Privacy Rings use zero-knowledge proofs, which let users prove they own and can spend a balance without revealing how much it holds.

A swap exchanges one token for another at the current market price. Instead of placing an order on an exchange and waiting for it to fill, the trader sends one token and receives another in a single transaction.

It has been revealed that swaps on Decrypt are powered by Jupiter, a Solana trading platform that offers swaps, lending, borrowing, perpetual futures and portfolio tools. Jupiter finds prices across Solana's trading venues, so users don't need to choose where a trade is executed.

At time of publication, swaps cover a select group of major cryptocurrencies and Solana tokens, as well as tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets.

As of November 2026, the Assets panel of the Portfolio page groups holdings into crypto, stocks, commodities and collectibles, and lists tokens including SOL, BTC, ETH, XRP and HYPE.

In a recent development, perpetual futures, or perps, are contracts that let traders bet on whether an asset's price will rise or fall without owning the asset. Unlike traditional futures, they have no expiry date. A trader who expects the price to rise goes "long," and one who expects it to fall goes "short.".

Recent findings suggest that perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets a trader control a larger position than their deposit would otherwise allow. Leverage magnifies gains and losses alike, and if the market moves against a position far enough, it can be liquidated, or closed automatically, wiping out the trader's margin.

Perps on Decrypt are powered by Phoenix, a fully onchain perpetuals exchange on Solana developed by Ellipsis Labs—making Decrypt the first media platform to offer perps trading alongside its journalism.

As of November 2026, Phoenix offers more than 100 perps markets on Decrypt, covering crypto, U.S. stocks, gold and pre-IPO companies. Markets trade around the clock, with leverage of up to 40x, according to Phoenix.

Decrypt looks to keep adding products to The Information Exchange, including Situation Rooms: pages that combine breaking news, live data, prices, probabilities and trading around a single subject.

Decrypt operates The Information Exchange, Decrypt Money Accounts and the swaps, perpetual futures and prediction market products described in this guide.

Industry observers note that perpetual futures are leveraged products and carry a high risk of loss. Availability may vary by region. Nothing in this guide is investment advice.

Tesla Cybertruck had its best month in over a year. It’s still going away

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that upcoming EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago.
  • Across all newly introduced vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.
  • It has been revealed that EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that upcoming EV prices edged up in October, but buyers still paid less than they did a year ago. The average transaction price for a new EV in the US was $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from October 2025, according to Kelley Blue Book, a Cox Automotive brand.

Across all newly introduced vehicles, the average hit a record $51,109, up 1.3% from September and 2.1% year over year, even as prices rose more slowly than they typically do in October.

It has been revealed that EV incentives barely budged from September’s revised 11.2% of the average transaction price to 11.3% in October. That’s up from 10.3% a year earlier and well above October’s industrywide average of 6.8%.

Tesla’s average selling price fell from September to $54,194, but it was still up 1.2% year over year. The Cybertruck helped push that average higher. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold 1,914 Cybertrucks in October, its best month in more than a year, at an average price of $92,380.

According to recent reports, the sad thing is that there likely is a market for an affordable electric pickup truck in the U.S. to compete with Ford’s F150 and others. The Ford Fathom may be the best fit for that market, now.

That sales bump comes as Tesla prepares to end Cybertruck production at its Austin factory in mid-2027. Elon Musk said Tesla will dismantle the assembly line around June or July to make room for more Cybercab robotaxis.

#167244. Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1067 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Lucid CEO admits it ‘did not even know where cars were’ and lost orders

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the tech giant’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.
  • Industry observers note that that’s a rough admission from a organization sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles.
  • Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lucid (LCID) CEO Silvio Napoli admitted on the tech giant’s Q3 earnings call that, as recently as this summer, the automaker “did not even know where cars were.” Buyers placed orders, Lucid took up to two weeks to locate and deliver a car, and some of those buyers walked away.

Industry observers note that that’s a rough admission from a organization sitting on thousands of unsold vehicles. And it’s a problem Tesla ran into, and fixed, back in 2018 at more than ten times Lucid’s current volume.

Napoli made the comment when an analyst asked whether Lucid’s deliveries would go up or down in the fourth quarter. He said that at the start of Q3, the company had orders where it “would take sometimes two weeks to deliver to the customer, and so we would lose the order.”.

He stated Lucid now has visibility on which cars are being built, where they’re shipped, where they’re stored, and when they can reach a customer. A new commercial team also now sells the cars it knows are available on the day a customer wants one.

Lucid built 3,228 more vehicles than it delivered in the first half of 2026, including 5,500 built but only 3,093 delivered in Q1. Its inventory hit $1.38 billion on the balance sheet at the end of June, which is why we reported earlier this year that Lucid had to adjust production after a bloated Q1 inventory.

So Lucid had thousands of cars on lots and in transit, and it was still losing buyers because it couldn’t match a car to an order fast enough.

Sources indicate that in Q3, Lucid cut production to 2,954 vehicles and delivered 3,806, down 7% year over year. Finished goods inventory fell by almost 15% during the quarter, according to new CFO Alexander De Bock. Inventory stood at $1.22 billion on September 30.

Tesla learned this lesson the hard way during the Model 3 ramp.

Recent findings suggest that by Q3 2018, Tesla was making roughly 4,000 Model 3s per week. That’s more cars every week than Lucid delivers in a full quarter today. Deliveries tripled or quadrupled in some markets, and the bottleneck moved from the factory to the trucks.

According to recent reports, elon Musk tweeted in September 2018 that Tesla had “gone from production hell to delivery logistics hell.” A week later, he remarked Tesla was facing an “extreme shortage of car carrier trailers” and had started building its own car carriers to keep cars moving. Tesla also rolled out door-to-door delivery and asked existing owners to help at delivery centers.

It didn’t stop there. In November 2018, with the federal tax credit about to be cut in half for Tesla buyers, Musk stated Tesla had bought trucking companies and locked in contracts with major haulers. Tesla moved cars east by truck instead of rail to cut weeks off transit times.

Tesla delivered 83,500 vehicles in Q3 2018, including 55,840 Model 3s, a record at the time.

When Model 3 reached Europe in February 2019, the first ship docked at Zeebrugge in Belgium and Tesla immediately had trouble processing the cars at the port.

According to recent reports, about a week after the first ship arrived, Tesla ended its contract with the organization preparing Model 3s at the port and took over the work itself. The target was 3,000 cars per week coming through one port.

Sources indicate that it worked. By March 2019, Tesla delivered more than 5,300 Model 3s in Norway alone, making it the best-selling car in the country by a wide margin. A car that’s sitting at a port or on a lot doesn’t make anyone money. Tesla treated delivery speed as a sales tool, not a back-office job.

We later learned from Musk himself that this “logistic hell” was almost the nail in Tesla’s coffin. The CEO said that Tesla was at the brink of bankruptcy at the time.

I like to think people were relatively patient with Tesla's growing pains when Model 3 was ramping up in 2018, largely because there weren't many alternatives for a sporty, relatively affordable EV.

But it's 2026. Buyers have plenty of options now, and the patience that early EV adopters once had for these kinds of mistakes is long gone.

This is one of the most embarrassing admissions we’ve heard on an earnings call, and credit to Napoli for saying it out loud. Most executives would have blamed “demand” and moved on.

Recent findings suggest that but it explains a lot. Lucid’s problem has never been the cars. The Air and Gravity are excellent products. The problem has been everything around them: service, software, and now we learn, basic inventory tracking. When you’re spending about $273,000 for every car you deliver, losing a buyer because you can’t find their car two weeks after they ordered is brutal.

It has been revealed that tesla solved this at 4,000 Model 3s a week while fighting for its own survival. Lucid is moving fewer than 300 cars a week. This isn’t a hard problem at that scale. It’s a discipline problem, and Napoli is right to call it that.

11 Best Aspen Hotels and Homes for Your Next Winter Getaway (2026)
