  • In a recent development, in an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that when Jennifer Lawrence joined Instagram in September, fans rejoiced at the idea of seeing more content from the actress known for her sarcastic humor and likable authenticity. What we didn’t see coming was the launch of her new hair care brand Mes° Beauty (pronounced “mess”) and the public backlash that followed.

In a recent development, in an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public. “She saw the numbers Rihanna, Selena Gomez, and Hailey Bieber were pulling in, and suddenly decided to join Instagram, too. Not necessarily to connect with her audience, but perhaps to tap into the same commercial machine and sell us even more stuff,” wrote one Instagram commenter.

It has been revealed that JLaw teamed up with Jasmina Aganovic, founder of biotech beauty company Arcaea Labs, to formulate the brand’s hair care. As they say, the proof is in the pudding, so when I was sent all three products in a PR mailer, I knew I wanted to put them to the test.

Read my full, honest review of Mes° Beauty’s hair mask, serum, and volume mist below.

Recent findings suggest that an intensive repair mask designed to be applied to dry hair anytime before washing. The milky-colored mask has a silky yet sticky, gelatin-like consistency that clings to your hair as you apply it. According to the brand, the mask prevents breakage and wash-day protein loss and protects the hair’s lipid barrier.

Industry observers note that the Multitask Repair Mask differs from other hair masks because you apply it before shampooing and can leave it on for five minutes or overnight. With such a wide treatment time, it might take some trial and error to find the “sweet spot” for your hair type. During my testing, I applied a generous coat of the mask 5 to 10 minutes before shampooing. The second time, I tried applying a thinner coat of the mask, then pinned my hair up with a claw clip for about two hours before rinsing it out. The longer you wear it, the better the results. I would recommend applying a light coat before going about your day; that way, the scent isn’t overpowering and it won’t drip on your clothes.

According to recent reports, after just two uses, my hair looked shinier and felt more hydrated after styling. As someone who rarely looks my hair care routine ahead of time, I appreciate that I can apply the mask just five minutes before I hop in the shower and still get noticeable results.

Recent findings suggest that although Mes° says the mask doubles as a styler for a glossy wet-hair look, I wouldn’t use it in that way. I think the product's consistency is too sticky and would be uncomfortable and messy (literally) to wear all day.

It has been revealed that some reviewers have mentioned a slightly off-putting smell. While the scent doesn’t bother me (it smells like a light, musky fragrance), it may not be for everyone. If I’m paying $52 for a hair mask, it would be nice to have a luxurious fragrance to add to the experience. If a brand is going to do musk, really lean into it with notes of sandalwood, amber, or patchouli.

The packaging also makes the product difficult to use. In the mailer I received, the mask comes in a GoGo Squeez-like pouch that you’re supposed to empty into the plastic tub. However, dipping my fingers into the tub felt clumsy, and next time I would just dispense directly from the pouch.

Industry observers note that A bi-phase serum that smooths frizz, restores shine, and provides heat protection up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit. The “bi-phase” claim comes from combining a lightweight oil and a serum in the formula. After touching it, applying it, and letting it sit in my hair for a few days, I think calling it a serum is misleading. The consistency and the way it applies are much more like a hair oil.

Sources indicate that on day two hair, I warmed two drops of the Off-Duty Restyling Serum between my palms, and worked it through my strands. I have very thick, straight, shoulder-length hair, so when I applied the serum up through my mid-lengths, it was way too oily. I don’t know if I would use it to restyle my hair unless I was planning to use a hot tool.

Industry observers note that I also tested the serum as a finishing product, applying it to my ends after blow-drying. I found this to be the most effective way to use the product on my hair type.

Overall, the Off-Duty Restyling Serum doesn’t make much sense to me. What’s the point of having heat protection if it’s made for “reshaping yesterday’s style?” Are we going back in with more heat? To me, that sounds like an extra step in my morning routine that I do not have the time or patience for.

It has been revealed that on days when I wash and blow-dry my hair, I like using a tiny amount of the serum just on my ends, and I've found it dries down nicely and leaves my hair soft and touchable. That remarked, I own other lightweight hair oils that work just as well for a fraction of the price—like FromLabs’ Protein Capsule Hair Repair Oil. If you have fine, wavy, or curly hair, the Off-Duty Serum may work better for you.

A lightweight spray that reduces scalp oiliness for lasting lift. Instead of creating gritty texture or absorbing excess oil like a dry shampoo, the Good Roots mist helps balance the scalp microbiome to produce less oil at the roots, extending the time until your next wash.

Over the past two weeks, I tested the Good Roots mist in three ways: applying it to damp hair before blow-drying, applying it to damp hair before air-drying, and applying it to dry day-two and day-three hair.

After about five uses of trial and error, I found it worked best when I applied it to my clean, damp roots and blow-dried. The heat felt like it helped dry down and “activate” the mist, whereas letting my hair air-dry didn’t produce much volume.

Pro-Tip: Be sure to hold the bottle about a foot away for even misting. The applicator pump doesn’t produce a fine spritz, and it took me a few uses to get that right.

According to recent reports, after two weeks of testing, the Good Roots Volume Mist is my favorite of the trio. Two key ingredients, the proprietary Arc-5 Technology and the Mediterranean microalgae, help support a balanced scalp, keeping your hair fresher longer. With consistent use, the Good Roots mist extended my time between hair washes—I typically wash every other day, but I was able to go a third day. Plus, the Juniperus virginiana oil in the formula has a fresh, woody scent that reminds me of a fancy sea salt spray.

According to recent reports, I also like that the mist doesn’t make my hair feel super gritty or textured the way a dry shampoo might. That remarked, I have other dry shampoo products that do a lot more heavy lifting than this volume mist. If I’m looking to achieve noticeable volume and lift in my thick hair, the Good Roots mist doesn’t cut it.

My general critique of Mes° Beauty is that the products are not very intuitive. They seem straightforward, but the brand doesn’t give great direction on how to get the most out of them. After the first one or two uses, you may feel they barely do anything at all. But if you learn how to use them properly when styling your hair, they can perform fairly well.

According to recent reports, mes° is supposed to be about “Less time fixing your hair. More time living,” but in reality, achieving that effortlessly chic, tousled look requires a fair bit of effort. In my opinion, this lineup is much more suited to someone who blows out or flat irons or curls their hair once or twice a week and wants to extend their style. For my hair type, these products don’t fit into my routine in a way that makes sense, but if you have fine and/or wavy hair, they might work better for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that genesis opened orders for the ultra-luxury electric SUV in South Korea, with prices starting at over $100,000. If you want coach doors, however, it will cost you a bit more.

Hyundai’s luxury brand is moving upscale with the GV90, its first fully electric three-row flagship SUV.

After unveiling the GV90 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco in August (which we had the pleasure to see firsthand), Genesis rolled out the newly introduced “ultra-luxe” SUV in its home market of Korea on Tuesday.

The Genesis GV90 introduces several “world-first” innovations, including the first independently opening and closing B-pillarless coach doors, a 12-airbag roof airbag system, and genuine wood floors with radiant heating.

It’s available in two models: the GV90 Standard with traditional swing doors and the GV90 Neolun, which features the “Neolun Arch Gate,” Genesis’ hidden B-pillar coach door system.

In Korea, the Genesis GV90 Standard 7-seater model starts at 139.5 million won, or about $104,000.

The GV90 Individual Lounge Seat (6-seater) starts at 145.5 million won ($108,500); the GV90 Neolun Standard (6-seater) starts at 189.9 million won ($141,500), while the top-spec GV90 Neolun Executive Suite (4-seater) starts at 239.5 million won ($178,500).

Based on Hyundai’s new eMP platform, developed exclusively for its flagships, Genesis mentioned the GV90 is like a “moving private lounge,” complete with a multi-chamber air suspension and a dual electronic limited-slip differential (E-LSD).

The platform is designed to open up interior space for the B-pillarless coach doors, swivel seats, and more.

When parked, the front seats swivel a full 180 degrees to face rear passengers or to create what Genesis calls “a face-to-face lounge-like configuration.”.

The interior is about as over-the-top as you could expect, with massive digital screens, premium materials, and plenty of luxury extras.

The GV90 is the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle to feature its new extendable display and the first Genesis model equipped with its next-gen Pleos Connect infotainment system.

Together, they create what Genesis calls a newly introduced realm of “display expandability.” While other vehicles, like the new Tucson and IONIQ 3, also use Pleos Connect, Hyundai developed an exclusive version for the GV90.

When the vehicle is parked, the screen can expand to 24.6″ at the push of a button, transforming it into a massive Cinematic Display.

Once extended, the display switches to Media Home mode, where you can watch Netflix, live TV, stream music, and more with third-party apps.

A mobile private theater wouldn’t be complete without a premium audio system, right? To top it off, Genesis added a 25-speaker Bang & Olufsen Premier 3D Sound System with Dolby Atmos, so it sounds like you’re actually at the movies.

In place of a traditional instrument cluster, the GV90 has a 25″ Head-Up Display (HUD) that indicates the vehicle’s speed, navigation directions, and other ADAS functions directly on the windshield.

In a recent development, the GV90 is also the first Hyundai Motor Group vehicle with a buttonless power system. When you enter the vehicle and close the door, the Motion Column Shifter moves from the 12 o’clock position to the 2 o’clock position.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the Crystal Sphere between the driver and passenger rotates to indicate it’s ready to drive. The vehicle starts when you press the brake.

It has been revealed that as a full-size flagship SUV, the Genesis GV90 is massive. It measures 208.1″ (5,285 mm) long, 79.9″ (2,030 mm) wide, and 71.5″ (1,815 mm) tall (71.4″ with 24″ tires), with a 127.8″ (3,245 mm) wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 (199.2″/5,060 mm in length) and Kia EV9 (197.4″/5,010 mm).

To power a full-size flagship SUV, it needs a significant battery. The GV90 uses a 123.5 kWh battery, the largest among Hyundai Motor’s EVs, which Genesis said provides a driving range of 500 km (310 miles) for the 7-seater version with 22″ wheels.

The GV90 Neonlun 6-seater with 24″ wheels has a range of up to 460 km (286 miles) on a single charge.

It’s equipped with a latest dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) system that delivers a combined 657 hp (490 kW) and 590 lb-ft (800 Nm) of torque, making it Hyundai Motor Group’s most powerful electric vehicle.

When using a 350 kW fast charger, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 22 minutes.

And.... once again Hyundai shortchanges the range. If you are going to drop a 200+ inch premium upright SUV into the market it requires a 140+ kwh battery (Rivian, BMW) to deliver segment appropriate range. You do not have to jump to a 200 kwh Escalade (though it is probably a better buy in every respect) but at least deliver 140+. Also, memo to powertrain engineering group: 350 kw is getting outdated on fast charging especially on a vehicle of this size. And while I am at it, what happened to the promised L3 ADAS? I think the 2028 Caddy is worth the wait compared to this.

“Thanks to the enthusiastic interest and support for the GV90 since its global premiere, we have begun full-scale sales in Korea first,” a Genesis official said, adding the flagship SUV will “set a newly introduced standard for luxury.”.

Following Korea, Genesis is expected to launch the GV90 in the US and other global markets in early 2027.

Genesis has yet to reveal US prices, but the GV90 Standard model is expected to start at around $100,000. The GV90 Neolun, on the other hand, will likely start closer to $150,000 or more.

According to recent reports, what do you think of the flagship Genesis GV90? Would you buy the standard version for about $100,000 or pay the extra for the Neolun with coach doors? Let us know in the comments.

Porsche CEO takes a shot at Tesla’s ‘flying’ Roadster stunt show

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche.
  • Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15.
  • Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that tesla’s “flying” Roadster just took a hit from Porsche. Speaking at a conference in Berlin today, CEO Michael Leiters remarked Porsche wants “to completely steer clear from any kind of effects and demonstrates,” according to Bloomberg.

Both automakers revealed their next halo cars on the same day, October 15. Tesla made a Roadster flip in mid-air. Porsche showed the Mission S, and Leiters says the two cars aren’t even chasing the same customers.

Tesla finally unveiled the next-gen Roadster last month, almost nine years after the 2017 prototype. The main event was a car using compressed-air thrusters to launch off a ramp, rotate in the air, and come back down on its wheels.

It was the payoff for months of hype. Musk spent most of the year promising a “flying” Roadster demo, and it slipped more than once. We reported in June that it had been pushed to August to make room for SpaceX thruster work.

There are three versions. The Performance trim uses suction fans and claims 0-60 mph in under 1.6 seconds, the Thrust trim adds rear cold-gas thrusters for a claimed sub-0.9-second run, and the single-seat Rocket trim gets thrusters all around the car and isn’t approved for public roads. Tesla gave no price and no production date, just Musk’s “2028, actually.”.

Sources indicate that porsche went the other way. Under the skin, the Mission S can take either a hybrid or a straight combustion powertrain. It’s a mid-engine car that sits above the 911 in the lineup, and well above it in price.

Leiters noted customer response has been “overwhelming” and that Porsche would rather show off real technical innovation than put on a show. If it reaches production, Ferrari is the obvious target, and Porsche hasn’t played in that segment since the 918 Spyder. Porsche is counting on a pricier, more exclusive lineup to rebuild its profits.

Sources indicate that not everyone in the supercar world agrees with Leiters. Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna rated Tesla’s Roadster launch “10 out of 10” last month.

Leiters has a point, even if Porsche pitching a gas and hybrid supercar as “technical innovation” in 2026 is a bit rich. But what bothers me more is who Tesla is aiming at.

It has been revealed that I’m concerned Tesla is starting to appeal to the lowest common denominator: people who watch a Roadster hop off a ramp and believe an actual flying car is coming. Musk pushed that idea himself. On Joe Rogan’s show, he called the upcoming demo “unforgettable” and said that if Peter Thiel wants a flying car, “we should be able to buy one.”.

In a recent development, that’s not real. Cold-gas thrusters work like a giant can of compressed air, and the math is brutal. The Rocket trim carries 400 liters of air at 10,000 psi, roughly 200 kg of gas. At the roughly 80 kN its rear thrusters produce, even a very efficient nozzle empties that tank in a few seconds. Then refilling it takes six to seven hours.

In a recent development, also someone on Bluesky pointed out that the video shows Mach diamonds in the exhaust stream of the thrusters. Which means it's so loud that anyone within 100 feet would suffer immediate and permanent hearing loss. This Roadster isn't useful for anything other than temporarily pumping stock prices.

So the Roadster’s “flying” will always be limited to stunts like this one. No hopping over traffic. No hovering. A couple of seconds of air, then a long wait at a compressor.

That’s great for a viral clip. But this is a car that dropped from a promised 620 miles of range in 2017 to “over 300” today, and Tesla would rather sell people on a flight the physics can’t deliver.

In a recent development, it’s hard for me to get excited for that. As a BEV enthusiast, I’m not more excited about Porsche’s ICE Mission S, but at least I trust Porsche to actually deliver that to customers.

Inside a Brooklyn Apartment That Feels Like an English Country Estate

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Set in a wide Brooklyn Heights brownstone, photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment, though modest in scale, gives the impression of a breakfast room in some well-appointed Cornish estate.
  • Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.
  • Industry observers note that just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Set in a wide Brooklyn Heights brownstone, photographer Ethan James Green’s apartment, though modest in scale, gives the impression of a breakfast room in some well-appointed Cornish estate. Hulking Victorian, Arts and Crafts, and Jacobean furniture dominates the space, Art Nouveau lamps aglow. The home draws an interesting contrast to the work for which he is best known—whether his black-and-white shoot with Kate Moss for Dazed or his recent Vanity Fair cover story with Carlos Alcaraz. Green’s apartment is, by comparison, more indicative of a bygone era, but it still reflects the irreverent, empathetic spirit at the heart of his practice.

The view from the bedroom into the living room.

Paintings by Raphael Soyer flank a portrait by Thomas Hart Benton in the living room; armchairs by George Mann Niedecken.

Industry observers note that just under 1,000 square feet, the one-bedroom unit serves dual purposes: to provide space to converge with his cherished friends and to house other faces that inspire him. Covering walls are the many 20th-century figurative paintings Green has gathered over the years, among them Social Realist portraits by Raphael Soyer, nudes both bold and tentative, and myriad depictions of introspective souls—images that captured Green in a spiritual grip.

According to recent reports, he displays the varied mix in interiors conceived with his friend Dylan Bailey, the Upcoming York–based artist and set designer, whom he met years ago on a shoot. Their collaboration was informal. Green would come home and find paint swatches left by Bailey, who might pop by and hang up a work while Green was shooting. The furniture they found at auction. “I wanted to have matching couches so when a friend comes over we can both take one, sink in, and talk,” says Green. The vintage sofas’ peach upholstery fits right in. “I didn’t realize until after getting them that the color showed up in several of the paintings,” Green says, referring to a portrait of an ironworker by Joseph Paul Vorst and a double nude by George Valentine Dureau.

A Victorian Renaissance Revival bed mingles with works by Maurice Grosser, Raphael Soyer, and Moses Soyer.

Green in the kitchen, surrounded by photographs.

It has been revealed that green grew up outside Grand Rapids, Michigan, surrounded by, as he recalls, “cornfields and dairy farms.” With missionary parents, unstructured days, and endless skies, he had the space and time to imagine a different life. “I knew I wanted to be a fashion photographer when I was 14 or 15, then found out I could model at 16,” he recalls. “I won the lottery. Modeling was a better way to learn than art school.” He moved to New York City at 17, the first student to graduate from his high school online. “I had to be here,” he states simply. “My first year in New York I shot with David Armstrong. He took me under his wing.”.

Now in his mid-30s, Green splits his time between the Significant Apple and Los Angeles with his boyfriend. On the East Coast, between shoots, he runs Latest York Life Gallery, opened in 2022 and named after the Chinatown insurance manufacturer across the street. His first show, dedicated to Baltimore-based photographer Steven Cuffie’s tender portraits of Black women, reflected Green’s devotion to his own medium and enduring interest in the variance of human faces. The 2023 exhibition “Sleeping Beauties” would blur the lines between Green’s life and work: Many of the paintings shown have come to reside in his apartment.

Green kneels before a bookshelf by Renzo Mongiardino in the bedroom, which is painted in a custom Benjamin Moore blue.

It has been revealed that portraits by Raphael Soyer and Leroy E. Mitchell Jr. flank The bedroom’s 19th-century French armoire, which reflects a view of another Soyer painting.

An Austrian Art Nouveau chandelier hangs in the living room, which displays paintings by (from left) Raphael Soyer, Joseph Paul Vorst, Raphael Soyer, and Hermann Grom-Rottmayer. The walls are painted in a custom Benjamin Moore color.

In a recent development, A 1949 self-portrait by Leroy E. Mitchell Jr., for instance, hangs in the bedroom. This was the first painting Green bought at auction, prior to which it had been found in a dumpster. Green’s research led him to Mitchell’s early life in Detroit, his community of peers, and his time as a teacher in Ghana. Meanwhile, one of Green’s most pedigreed finds, a painting by Thomas Hart Benton, whose 1931 mural of industrial workers hangs in The Met, stoked another uncovering. “I had gotten multiple paintings and then realized many of the artists knew each other or were friends,” he says, noting that Benton and Vorst were studio mates. It is like Green is uncovering a parallel life of creatives finding true kinship.

Industry observers note that green Crowned the kitchen cabinet with art, including works by Raphael Soyer, Robert Philipp, and David Armstrong. To its right hang photographs by (from top) Nan Goldin, David Armstrong, and Richard Avedon.

Framed family snapshots fill the hallway shelves.

It is these serendipitous journeys into the lives of other artists that Green cherishes as much as the art itself. “I love paintings,” he says. Perhaps a bit too much? Bailey would tease him that every time he arrived there was yet another portrait to place. “The reason there’s one hanging on the mirror over the mantel is because I had no more wall space,” Green says. As he explains, his collection, like his life and work, is ultimately about affection. “You cannot be a good photographer without being empathetic,” Green observes. “I love people. I love faces.” He’s made sure that love is hard to miss.

Running shorts with sweat-wicking fabric are the way to go, Katz indicates. The inseam is the length from the crotch to the bottom. A longer length will show less skin but may disrupt the range of motion, while some running shorts favorites, like the Lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short, offer a 2.5-inch option if you like a mini fit.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s new electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

Sources indicate that toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

Recent findings suggest that after launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

Starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, stated (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s new EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

While she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

According to recent reports, the Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average latest vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a latest vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

You can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

Industry observers note that thinking about making the switch to an EV? With the 2027 models at dealerships, now could be a good time to find a deal on current 2026 models. You can use the links below to see what’s available at Toyota and Subaru dealerships near you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that BACK PAIN DOESN'T care about your substantial looks to sail through life in comfort, making it hard to do everything from getting in a workout to sitting at your computer. Relief can come in many forms, including regularly stretching and strengthening the surrounding muscles, but sometimes, it can also involve using one of the best inversion tables to ease pressure on your back.

Recent findings suggest that “An inversion table is a device that allows you to hang at an angle, or even upside down, with your feet secured,” explains Max Shlykov, MD, an orthopedic spine surgeon at the Maryland Spine Center. “This position stretches and decompresses the spine and surrounding muscles.”.

It’s notable to get this out of the way now: An inversion table won’t magically cure your back pain or fix the underlying cause of it. But it can temporarily ease your pain and the tension that’s contributing to it. Inversion tables tend to be especially helpful for people with chronic back concerns like herniated discs, sciatica, degenerative disc disease, muscle spasms, or general stiffness, according to Shayan Ghadamabadi, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University Health Care Physical & Occupational Therapy.

Industry observers note that the best inversion tables are sturdy enough to support your height and weight, with adjustable hanging angles, Dr. Shlykov says. “Models that are more lightweight may be easier on your back to use and set up,” he adds.

Sources indicate that you’re not born knowing how to pick an inversion table, making it important to choose wisely. Here’s what to consider when looking for one of these pain-relieving tools, plus sturdy options to try. Because you need to know how to actually use one of these tables, we included advice for beginners to help put you on the right path to greater comfort.

Teeter’s FitSpine X3 Inversion Table hits all our best marks thanks to its durability, extended ankle lock handles, and secure, comfortable fit. The device is made with heat-treated steel for unmatched strength and support, and the foam backrest prevents your body from slipping or sliding while inverted, according to Dr. Wallace.

It has been revealed that the comfortable table is lined with acupressure nodes to target and release trigger points, and Dr. Wallace states the FlexTech bed moves with your body to enhance decompression and improve range of motion. You can also rest assured about safety features, as the patented wrap-around ankle cups are secure and supportive. Dr. Mesiwala says this is crucial for proper relaxation and effectiveness. What’s more, the lumbar bridge can help release lower back tension and alleviate glute pain triggered by sciatica.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll also get access to a free personal training app with a library of video and audio guides for on and off the inversion table, Dr. Verma states. The only qualm? It may be difficult or time-consuming to assemble.

Read More: The Best Compression Boots, Tested By Us.

Sources indicate that the Innova ITX9900 Heavy Duty Inversion Therapy Table is a budget-friendly option that doesn’t compromise on quality, according to Dr. Wallace. It offers a six-position adjustable pin system for safety locking and consistent inversion, a large, padded backrest, and soft-touch foam handlebars for easy access to getting in and out of position, he notes. This table is great for anyone, but it’s particularly good for beginners thanks to its ease of use and adjustable headrest, height, and footrest.

It has been revealed that this inversion table also features a True Balance System, which helps users find their center of gravity for smooth, seamless inversion. Not only will this maximize tension release, but it can also improve spinal decompression. Another pro: The headrest is adjustable, too.

Sources indicate that when it comes to getting a full, comfortable stretch, the EP-560 is a safe bet. It features patented wrap-around ankle supports, an ergonomic T-grip ankle lock, and an easy-dial foot platform for a more comfortable, secure fit. The backrest is also a game-changer. Most inversion tables use a simple foam material; the EP-560 ComforTrak backrest is designed to reduce friction and enhance spinal stretch and decompression. We also love that it’s pretty customizable. It comes with built-in tools for easy adjustability, including a Lumbar Bridge for deeper traction on the lower back and Acupressure Nodes that target muscle tension.

Recent findings suggest that the device is made out of an ultra-durable, heat-treated steel, adding an extra layer of strength and support. If you’re a little closer to the 300-lb range, this is a solid option.

It’s on the pricier side, but the Harison Electric Inversion Table is a top pick for both Dr. Mesiwala and Dr. Verma thanks to its adjustable footbed, memory-foam backrest, and heavy-duty build. The device is made with seamless welding and a steel frame to support up to 350 pounds, and the ergonomic ankle lock design is supportive without feeling too tight or restrictive. Security is also a top priority, and the table includes a high-quality safety belt that allows you to strap in while inverted (on top of the secure ankle holders).

The table is heavier than other options on this list, but it’s foldable for easy storage. It also includes a 30-day trial and replacement of spare parts within one year for no extra cost.

Read More: The Best Massage Guns, Tested By Us.

If you’re looking for an inversion table that doubles as a massager, here’s your pick. The vertical massage pad covers the entire spine with a contoured lumbar pad for a close-up massage and vibrating sensation, and the in-unit heating pad provides warmth to the lower back. There are also multiple mode settings to suit your massage and heat preferences, and the included user manual provides all necessary instructions and details.

This model has a new, improved ankle-holding system to reduce pressure on the ankles when inverted, while still ensuring a secure, protective fit. There’s also a six-position pin system on the side of the machine that lets you adjust the angle without dismounting the device.

According to recent reports, each inversion table accommodates different heights, so it's vital to read the fine print. The Teclor Inversion Table adjusts to fit people up to 6'8", making it a good option for taller consumers. It also can support up to 350 pounds, one of the largest weight capacities you’ll find.

Sources indicate that this is a relatively simple inversion table, and the low price supports that. But you’ll still get a comfortably padded back, cushioned handles, and an easy-to-reach handle for adjustability. The ankle-holding system is thickly padded, too. A double-locking system helps to ensure your device is firmly in place when it’s in use. When you’re done inverting, it folds up small enough to stash in a closet.

Read More: The 6 Best Compression Boots to Support Muscle Recovery.

Consider the Teeter FitSpine LX9 the slightly more luxurious version of our top pick, the X3. This has all the elements owners love about the X3, including that durable heat-treated steel frame and padded back, but in a slightly sleeker, user-friendly design. The LX9 has an eight-point floating suspension system for a large range of motion, along with reinforced padded handles for a comfortable grip.

In a recent development, enjoy eight acupressure nodes to help relieve muscle tension while you hang. The included lumbar bridge is adjustable and works to tweak your hip alignment. The LX9 has a step-through design with a specialized boarding platform to make it easy to get on and off. There’s even a built-in storage caddy to hold your gear while you invert.

Using an inversion table isn’t as simple as diving into a new set of dumbbells. These devices require you to move your body upside-down, making it important to know what you’re doing and how to ease into the process.

Sources indicate that it’s notable to start with a “modest” angle vs. going into a full-out inversion when you’re starting out, according to Raymond Agostino, DPT, owner of Agostino Athletics in Fort Myers, Florida. “The goal is to introduce your body to the position and create a gentle traction effect without overwhelming your system,” he claims.

Sources indicate that agostino suggests starting with a gentle recline, like 20 to 25 degrees for 30 to 45 seconds and see how you feel. “If you feel comfortable and don't experience dizziness, increased pain, or other symptoms, you can gradually increase the time or angle over future sessions,” he says. Agostino recommends only changing one variable at a time—angle and inversion time—to ease yourself in. “You don't need to go farther upside down and stay there longer all at once,” he says.

When you’re inverted, you may feel a pressure sensation in your head or a mild “head rush,” Agostino says. “When your head is positioned below your heart, blood pressure and pressure within the eyes can increase, which is one reason inversion feels very different from simply lying flat,” he explains. You might also feel a feeling of fullness in your head or facial pressure. “Those sensations should remain mild and should resolve when you return upright,” according to Agostino.

In a recent development, agostino points out that you don’t get a trophy for going completely upside down. “If a smaller angle provides the stretch or relief you're looking for, there may be no reason to progress to a full inversion,” he indicates.

According to recent reports, safety is paramount when shopping for an inversion table. "It’s ideal to find a product with comfortable ankle straps and safety locks to keep you secure and in place," says Kushagra Verma, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine surgeon at DISC Sports and Spine Center. You also want to make sure the table can be controlled and manipulated by the user if you proposal to use the device alone. Inversion tables should be used with caution, especially if you’re a beginner, says Rahul Shah, MD, a board-certified orthopedic spine and neck surgeon at Premier Orthopaedic Associates. Additionally, older adults and those who have chronic dizziness, high blood pressure, glaucoma, inner ear problems, heart disease, and/or severe injuries should avoid inversion tables without talking to their doctor first, he says. Keep this in mind, too, per Agostino: “A little pressure may be expected. Feeling like something is wrong is not something you need to train yourself to tolerate.” If it feels like your back pain is worsening, or if you develop fresh numbness, tingling, weakness, or radiating pain, Agostino recommends that you stop using the inversion tale.

Industry observers note that sturdiness and durability are crucial for preventing accidents or instability while you’re upside down, Dr. Verma claims. He recommends always looking for a product made with high-quality materials, such as stainless steel, to provide better support and longevity. Be sure to read customer reviews and seek expert opinions on the machine's sturdiness when shopping. Of course, all the selections on our list have been vetted in this way.

In addition to safety features, all experts agree that it’s crucial to consider how much weight an inversion table can safely hold. (The machine should clearly state this in the product description.) Because the machine puts you in a rather compromising position, maximum weight capacity is key for keeping you safe and at ease, Dr. Shah notes. Going over the weight capacity raises the odds that the table will break or flip while you’re on it, potentially injuring you in the process, Agostino says.

It’s key to consider the table's length to ensure it accommodates your size and height, notes Ali Mesiwala, MD, a neurosurgeon and complex spine expert at DISC Sports and Spine Center. Most inversion tables are adjustable for a customized fit, but it’s best to ensure the maximum height is within your range for effective use. The width of the table is another key factor, as a wider table can offer more stability during inversion, particularly if you’re on the taller or heavier side, says Brian Wallace, DC, a chiropractor at Pinewood Family Care. As a general rule of thumb, the width of the table should be wide enough for your core to conformably fit and not fall to either side, Dr. Shah adds.

Industry observers note that depending on your needs, different inversion tables include add-on features like lumbar spine support, heat, memory foam, or massage elements, Dr. Wallace says. These extra features are not a necessity, but they can be beneficial if you’re looking for added comfort and therapeutic benefits, he says. Just remember: extra add-ons should be considered second to the table's fundamental stability, comfort, and safety.

It has been revealed that an inversion table isn’t the cheapest tool you’ll use to reduce your back pain, but there is a range to consider. Most tables will run you anywhere from $150 to $450, with higher-priced models having additional features like heat, memory foam, and massage.

To track down the best inversion tables, Men’s Health editors, including contributor Korin Miller, consulted three orthopedic surgeons, a neurosurgeon, a chiropractor, and two physical therapists to learn more about the important features to look for in an inversion table. From there, we looked at the most popular inversion tables on the market and narrowed the field based on our experts’ requirements. Each inversion table was ranked based on factors such as size, weight capacity, and safety features. In a recent development, the best time to use an inversion table is typically when your muscles are relaxed, such as after a workout at the end of the day, indicates Dr. Wallace. You can also put your arms on the support bars. Essentially, you should do whatever feels comfortable to you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the newly introduced IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.
  • Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the upcoming IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.
  • While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the newly introduced IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai announced its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the upcoming IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

Recent findings suggest that it uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

Recent findings suggest that that’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

According to recent reports, hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a new Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

The 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

On the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an update. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Industry observers note that hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the new Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

With the 2027 models on the way, you may be able to score some deals on Hyundai’s current EV lineup. Want to see what’s available near you? You can use the links below to find available Hyundai IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 models near you, along with any current offers.

#167209. Breaking: Are AI Design Visualizers Selling Us on Slop?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1653 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Architecturaldigest ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Are AI Design Visualizers Selling Us on Slop?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that can I interest you in an autonomous sauna rideshare?
  • Recent findings suggest that friends, do I even need to say it?
  • The slopject’s unsavory first cousin, the slopspace—a full-scale interior scheme, created through digital rendering, and now generative AI—is increasingly populating home-decor inspiration sites like this one, where a viewer can encounter improbable living scenarios like garage apartments with no ladders or stairs to reach the lofted bed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that can I interest you in an autonomous sauna rideshare? How about a conversation pit car? Or a Magic 8 Ball in the shape of Rick Rubin? How about a plate for a single almond or a toilet turntable?

Recent findings suggest that friends, do I even need to say it? These objects—or slopjects, as their creator calls them—are not real. Though they look convincing on the feed, they don’t exist in meatspace the way that you or I do. They are Dadaist fantasies, dreamed up and rendered digitally without the limitations of production budgets, market demand, or even those pesky things known as laws.

The slopject’s unsavory first cousin, the slopspace—a full-scale interior scheme, created through digital rendering, and now generative AI—is increasingly populating home-decor inspiration sites like this one, where a viewer can encounter improbable living scenarios like garage apartments with no ladders or stairs to reach the lofted bed.

With hyperrealistic renderings a mere prompt away (and disclosures of AI-generated content remaining spotty at best), it’s getting harder to tell what’s real. On platforms like Pinterest and Instagram, where homeowners often seek inspiration for their design projects, the speculative images that float through the digital ether can be particularly hard to detect. Entire subreddits are dedicated to sniffing them out.

And detection is just the beginning. Aside from struggling to detangle fact from fiction in stumbled-upon images, consumers are also using LLMs—or large language models, AI tools designed to work with human speech—to generate their own visions of their dream home, without always understanding what it takes to make those fantasies a reality. That dynamic is starting to have concrete consequences for the professionals charged with designing and building the rooms we live in, where dollars and cents, artisanal skill, and the laws of physics remain painfully real. (Just ask the guy who tried to exit the lofted bed without a ladder.).

“People are seeing or prompting more fantastical solutions that are not rooted in the reality of the built environment, and then they’re presenting those to us as something that can be executed,” says Kevin Greenberg, founder and principal of the AD PRO Directory–listed firm Space Exploration Design. “We do it diplomatically and we do it politely, but we will tell them, ‘Oh, you know, it’s really difficult to achieve a stone ceiling.’”.

In a recent development, this change is happening fast. Stanford University’s 2026 AI Index Report notes that more than half of the population has started using generative AI in the past three years—a swiftness that outpaces both personal computers and the internet itself. When Midjourney and other AI imaging tools first hit the market, Greenberg indicates, clients used them to test the limits of what was aesthetically possible. “The prompt was like, ‘tropical Tudor fantasy,’ and then we were left to clean up the mess,” he recalls. “The images we were seeing were just tacky, and we all got a really substantial belly laugh out of it.” No one’s laughing now, he says.

These days, homeowners are feeding designer-created collages, mood boards, and sketches into Claude to see what spaces might look like once they’re built. The results tend to be uncanny: surfaces gleam like the Las Vegas strip, proportions are wonky, and there’s an unsettling feeling of dead air. Cy and Genevieve Carter, the principals of the Fresh York City–based interiors firm Carter Design, joke that the worst dig they can make on a space is to say it feels like standing inside of a rendering. In the world of AI images, “there’s not a simplicity of space,” indicates Genevieve, which often means that more subtle textures like plaster don’t properly register.

Jake Shapiro, the owner of Hudson Valley–based millwork studio Slabrock, compares the images produced through AI software to the bloodless cuisine now rendered on deli signs. “It looks like scrambled eggs, but it also looks like H.P. Lovecraft, and that’s just horrific,” he states. “The same thing exists in design.”.

There’s treachery in these images, designers agree, in that they portray a space nearly—but not quite—photorealistically. While that theoretically might help a homeowner understand how a designer’s vision for a space maps onto the real thing, it also bakes in a false sense of exactness that can leave room for misunderstanding or even disappointment. Organic materials like wood, for instance, can be difficult to predict with precision in AI. Every tree is different, Shapiro points out.

Catherine Campbell Pearson, a set designer and stylist based in Brooklyn, is seeing AI-fantasy expectations infiltrate the environments she designs for photoshoots too. In the past she and her clients would work from a “comp,” or a Photoshopped portrayal of the imagined end shoot. With those more lo-fi pictures, there was an understanding that the finished product would look slightly different. That’s disappearing in the age of GenAI: “It’s such a cohesive version of their idea that there’s much more attachment to the finished product looking exactly like this AI image.”.

This phenomenon has real consequences for designers, whose expertise is on the line when a rendering goes awry. When clients go off on their own and submit designers’ early proposals into AI platforms, “The rendering that it produces is really unsexy and clunky and ugly,” states Greenberg. “Then they’re looking at us like, ‘Well, you’re actually not that good at your job.’”.

What these examples illustrate isn’t a new problem, exactly, but it is one that’s more apparent in the age of AI. Just as Pearson has relied on low-resolution comps to create environments in the past, designers often use tools like collage, drawings, and mood boards to gesture at vibe and design intent before progressing to a more dialed-in rendering. But most homeowners don’t have the language to communicate exactly what they want to a designer—and when they do, the language may not precisely match the listener’s interpretation. (One person’s “cozy” interior is another’s clutter-filled nightmare, just as one person’s “serene” oasis is another’s sterile dystopia.).

Recent findings suggest that LLMs offer clients a way to articulate their ideas in a way they may not have been able to otherwise—but in doing so, they create a highly specific rendering for a space that will require negotiation with real materials, labor, and budget—the latter being a serious constraint where AI can cause problems, states Tyler Polich, cofounder of the Los Angeles–based firm Years Studio. He shares an example of a client fiddling with an image and generating an element fully clad in copper—an option he and his partner would have never presented because of the cost. “Maybe it makes for a compelling image,” he concedes, “but we know that Gemini just blew their budget immediately.”.

In certain cases, these visualizations can simplify things for designers and clients. Lucca Zeray, the Berkshires-based maker of Lucca House modular shelving, has found the addition of an AI rendering tool—a “configurator” that can depict his brand’s color-edged units in the proportions they’re seeking and provide a cost estimate—to be a game changer in the ordering process. “It’s a way that we can be like, ‘Here, you draw it,’ and close the gap,” he notes. Unlike the every-detail-on-the-table possibilities of a full interior design rendering, Zeray’s configurator is only manipulating a few straightforward options, which might be part of the reason for its success.

According to recent reports, in the reality of a built design, image making is only a small piece of the puzzle. The real work is in executing—navigating the personal relationships, sourcing fabricators, and negotiating details with the give and take of material reality. “We don’t work just in ideas,” says Genevieve Carter. “We work in stuff and things, and people, and their expertise is still a dialogue.”.

Beyond the making itself, the design still needs to be good. Before AI was widely adopted, the algorithm-fueled flattening of taste was already in the cultural crosshairs. Social platforms reward likeable, heavily publicized images, like Athena Calderone’s marble-wrapped Brooklyn kitchen—photos that have been shared again and again. The problem then becomes that everyone is asking for an Athena Calederone–style kitchen. (It’s worth noting that even Calderone herself seems to have moved on from this look, by the way—her most recent home tour features a much moodier, Art Deco–inflected interior.) In today’s technological climate, this dilemma is taking a new form, as visuals take shape based on all of the environments that have been photographed and put online. But, says Polich, there’s an inherent flaw in this system: “The vast amount of visual information is relatively mediocre.” Real estate websites, DIY blogs, e-commerce images—most of the internet doesn’t look like, well, AD. It’s designed to be crowd-pleasing and just fine, not necessarily something extraordinary or innovative.

Years Studio similarly seeks to tease out its clients’ personalities—“something that is real and human and only exists in them,” as Polich puts it. That’s a vulnerable undertaking, but also one that AI cannot replicate when its foundation is built on remixing what’s already come before. Greenberg, the Carters, and Polich all recognize that there’s some element of a trust fall required on the client’s side. By the end of a project, a designer is often familiar with the most intimate details of their client’s life—even what they keep in their nightstand. (They see those specialty chargers, and they don’t judge.).

But in earning trust, ironically, AI is also occasionally lending designers an assist. For the Carters, an exacting client was reassured in the studio’s recommendation of a particular stone after she’d exhausted all of the other options herself in her AI engine of choice. Another time, they won over a prospect by tweaking his AI rendering, and suggesting color options the client hadn’t considered. Is it possible that Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini could remind homeowners why they hired a designer in the first place? Just ask the Rick Rubin Magic 8 ball: Signs point to yes.

#167208. Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1035 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a fresh batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Industry observers note that it’s a rare data point.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a fresh batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

Industry observers note that it’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its new Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, demonstrates four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

It has been revealed that HMD took its first truck on November 2 and notes it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler said Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

The company ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

Owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Tesla debuted volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It says the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

So we’re left with proxies. Tesla indicates its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how significant that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

Sources indicate that the order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Recent findings suggest that tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that reveals whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

I think the semi is going to be a major seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk now indicates Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first declared it was killing it.
  • The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a company that sells cars to people.
  • In a recent development, on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk now indicates Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first declared it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a company that sells cars to people.

In a recent development, on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027.

The reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of plan, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

Recent findings suggest that and the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

Tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

In a recent development, some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

Sources indicate that the most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”.

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”.

That’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t revealed a single new consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that launched in 2017 and 2020.

Tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

Even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

The pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car looks for Robotaxi in 2024. No newly introduced consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

According to recent reports, A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

Recent findings suggest that tesla is becoming a company that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

BYD’s full-size luxury SUV has a wheel problem, and it’s fixing it for free

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its upcoming full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.
  • The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.
  • It has been revealed that after opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its upcoming full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

It has been revealed that after opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a new record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD said the problem stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

It has been revealed that the manufacturer stated it “immediately” debuted an investigation and corrected the matter so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a upcoming visual error-prevention mechanism to limit concerns like this going forward.

BYD noted the problem does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

According to recent reports, the company remarked owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD said, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

It has been revealed that the Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

In a recent development, all versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

In a recent development, in comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

According to recent reports, based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li mentioned the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

  • Recent findings suggest that this ability to infuse varied mediums in your house isn’t reserved for just the Grammy-winning artists of the world; as long as you know where to look, weaving photography into your home is quite an attainable undertaking.
  • Want to display high-quality artistic photographs without breaking the bank?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photos have the power to add personality to your home’s art collection, showcasing a distinct mood or point of view while boosting your space’s aesthetic. Alicia Keys and Swizz Beatz’s San Diego home is a masterclass in this craft. Among the antique African woodwork and abstract ceramics sit carefully placed Gordon Parks photographs that layer in a new, thought-provoking dimension to the artwork in their home.

Recent findings suggest that this ability to infuse varied mediums in your house isn’t reserved for just the Grammy-winning artists of the world; as long as you know where to look, weaving photography into your home is quite an attainable undertaking. Below, we’ve rounded up our favorite places to buy prints online. Whether you’re searching for a one-of-one vintage photograph, a tool to help you exhibit your own snaps, or a photo collection that removes the guesswork from the curation process, these sites can help you add a personal touch to your interiors.

Want to display high-quality artistic photographs without breaking the bank? Desenio can help. The site offers contemporary and abstract art prints that can add visual interest to modern interiors, and many of the pieces cost far less than $100. Add natural sophistication with a dramatic leaf print or evoke a sense of intimacy with a close-up portrait of the human form. With multiple sizes and frames available, you can snag a couple of smaller photos to complete your gallery wall, or make a statement with one large print to hang over a bed or sofa.

It’s a shame for those candid moments among friends and stunning vacation sunsets to stay trapped and largely unseen in your phone’s camera roll. That’s where Framebridge comes in, printing your images onto high-quality photo paper and encasing them in custom frames. The company also offers photo layouts with life-size hanging guides to help you wall-mount your images with the accuracy and precision that they deserve. Essentially, Framebridge streamlines the entire framing process to be easy and accessible, elevating family photos and artistic stills alike.

If you’re a fine art aficionado who is hoping to track down rare finds, 1stDibs is the platform for you. While it also sells vintage and designer furniture, the fine art photography collection is unmatched. You can purchase pieces from legendary fashion photographers, like this signed portrait of Whoopi Goldberg by Annie Leibovitz, as well as avant-garde photographs like “Africaine, No. 2,” by Shawn Theodore. With photographs and photo books spanning styles and price points, it’s easy to get lost in a sea of beautiful images. Use the brand’s curated pages to narrow your search to specific focuses, like color photography or figurative photography.

If you’re a homesick West Coaster or an East Coaster with California dreams, your next piece should come from Lndn Gray. Peruse the site for landscape photography that embodies the surrealist loneliness of the Pacific shores or for a still life that romanticizes the raucous rock-star culture of Los Angeles. You can select from a variety of print sizes and frame options. Add a decidedly Western flair by pairing these prints with your favorite cowhide rug or leather couch.

Artfully Walls is the perfect destination for those who don’t know where to start their search for high-quality, wall-enhancing prints. It features a huge volume of works from a trove of emerging artists worldwide. If a high level of choice overwhelms you, or you simply want an expert’s opinion, take advantage of Artfully Walls’ collections of ready-to-hang art, curated by designers and industry professionals. Louisa Tratalos, founder of British interior design brand Colours of Arley, has an Artfully Walls collection that includes this print featuring colorful, Scandinavian-style architecture by Dutch photographer Sander Groenendijk. Or browse picks selected by Justin Huxol of Huxhux Designs, including this whimsical “sponge cake” photo by Julie Vielvoije.
