Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • Recent findings suggest that UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

Recent findings suggest that UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This latest study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

Sources indicate that this was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

Recent findings suggest that UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

Sources indicate that the researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

Industry observers note that when the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is key to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

Recent findings suggest that “Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more crucial to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She noted that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is vital to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

According to recent reports, “I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.

#167135. The Courage to Disagree

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Courage to Disagree

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • At 23, Mike Soutar was appointed editor of the British teen pop magazine Smash Hits.
  • Recent findings suggest that soutar was much younger than editors working on other titles; in fact, he was younger than almost everyone on his own team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

At 23, Mike Soutar was appointed editor of the British teen pop magazine Smash Hits. It was an amazing opportunity at such a young age for someone who had left school and started life as a journalist just six years earlier.

Recent findings suggest that soutar was much younger than editors working on other titles; in fact, he was younger than almost everyone on his own team. Feeling the need to be seen as a strong, decisive leader, he modeled himself on the powerful authority figures he had seen in Hollywood movies.

Recent findings suggest that his leadership was falling flat, and after a couple of weeks, the organisation’s CEO, Sir Robin Miller, visited him. Sir Robin gave Soutar some advice that has stuck with him to this day: “A great day in the office is when I lose more arguments than I win.".

What initially seemed counterintuitive—how can you assert authority if you are constantly shown to be wrong?—became a central mantra for a career that took Soutar to the pinnacle of the media world.

Industry observers note that encouraging disagreement lies at the heart of Soutar’s definition of a great leader. Why, if disagreement can be so valuable, are we often so reluctant to challenge each other?

Many of us naturally like the easy life. It’s tempting to keep our heads down, get on with our work, and avoid being marked as a troublemaker.

In her research into speaking truth to power, Professor Megan Reitz, leadership expert and author of Speak Out, Listen Up, has explored why people remain silent, even when they have something important to contribute.

According to recent reports, reitz told me about a leader who was frustrated that employees weren't speaking up and assumed they needed to become more assertive or articulate. But when she and her colleagues spoke to those employees, one response revealed a rather different problem: "Last time somebody spoke up around here, they disappeared.".

Sources indicate that the issue wasn't a lack of courage. It was what people believed might happen if they challenged authority. As Reitz explained, our willingness to express an opinion depends not just on our own confidence, but on how the person listening behaves and how safe they make us feel.

Growing awareness of the need for psychological safety has led leaders to tell their teams it’s OK to speak up and challenge. But telling people they have a safe space isn’t enough; you have to demonstrate it. Trust develops through repeated interactions and consistent behaviour.

When Mike Soutar reflected on the advice he took from Sir Robin Miller, he explained how he saw a culture of positive dissent in the workplace evolving.

“It starts with trust so that everybody knows that they can voice their feelings, their doubts, their own opinions.

From there, it moves into constructive dissent, where ideas are challenged rather than individuals attacked. Then it moves into decision-making, where the leader weighs the arguments and reaches a conclusion.

Finally, you move to accountability, where the leader parcels out the jobs, timelines, and deadlines, with everybody getting behind the decision that's been made.

When I understood this, it transformed my capabilities as a leader because it meant I could take people with me.”.

Building constructive dissent on a foundation of trust creates an environment where people actively seek alternate opinions to create better outcomes, rather than spiraling into a destructive culture of blame and competition.

Disagreement that leads to better decisions ultimately strengthens working relationships, creating a positive cycle that reinforces a safe space for dissent.

The ability to challenge and dissent doesn’t mean you will always get your way, but you should always be heard. That only works when the leader genuinely engages, listens, and is seen to welcome challenge.

Soutar later moved into his first managing director role at the London dance radio station Kiss FM, where one of his first moves was to change the station’s playlist policy. He wanted the station to focus on playing only "fresh" music—nothing more than two years old. To mark the shift, he planned a symbolic bonfire of old records in the station’s car park.

The proposal provoked strong opposition among both staff and listeners, who felt that Soutar was destroying a culture they cared deeply about. People warned him, but he dismissed their criticism.

According to recent reports, “We didn't end up having a bonfire. I’m glad this happened before social media existed, because I think I would have been hounded out of a job.

Sources indicate that all around me, I had people telling me in advance, ‘This is a really bad idea’. And I didn't listen to them because I took it personally.”.

Knowing that constructive dissent matters is one thing, but welcoming it when your own judgment is being questioned is quite another. A culture of dissent has to be source-agnostic, focusing on the idea itself rather than the person who suggested it.

Industry observers note that professor Reitz, whose research explores speaking truth to power, warns that leaders often underestimate the signals they send when challenged. They may genuinely believe they are approachable, yet their colleagues experience something quite different.

According to recent reports, reitz calls these behaviours "shut-up signals," the often-unintentional gestures and responses that discourage people from speaking openly. She describes how her own "thinking face" can become a frown when she's particularly interested in a conversation. Someone who doesn't know her might interpret that expression as disapproval.

Sources indicate that the danger is particularly acute when someone challenges a leader's judgment. As Reitz warns, "If you respond poorly, you can just forget about ever getting difficult feedback again.".

Leaders need to respond to dissent with curiosity rather than judgment. Seek to uncover why someone disagrees and what they might see differently.

Recent findings suggest that we can often react too swiftly, shutting down debate without taking time to reflect. Even if the challenge isn’t ultimately accepted, a good leader will return to the person who flagged an alternative approach, acknowledge their contribution, and explain what they have decided.

Demonstrating that their perspective was considered and valued reinforces trust and encourages them to try again.

Sir Robin Miller made a huge impact on the young Mike Soutar when he said, “A great day in the office is when I lose more arguments than I win.” He helped Soutar recognise that effective leaders don’t need to win every argument, but that better decisions come when you invite dissent.

Constructive dissent requires challenge on both sides: the courage to challenge and the courage to invite challenge.

When was the last time someone challenged your thinking, and what did your response teach them about whether they should do so again?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Zonveer ZX3 is one of the best values I’ve seen in electric off-road riding, and one of the most fun things I’ve ridden to date – value for the dollar. Its Black Friday sale brings the 2,800W electric dirt bike down to $1,299, $500 off its $1,799 list price.

In a recent development, for that money, you get a 1,200Wh battery, dual hydraulic disc brakes, and full suspension in a 130 lb package. That’s a great entry point for beginners.

Zonveer is a young brand. It released in the US in March with two bikes, the kid-sized DX1 and the ZX3, and it’s run by United Mobility, which lists its address in Dover, Delaware. It sells direct and ships from US warehouses, and Zonveer also sells the ZX3 across Europe under its own brand through its EU store.

Here’s what the ZX3 brings, according to Zonveer’s product page:.

A hub motor means there’s no motor chain to maintain, and the NFC card and PIN unlock mean there’s no app to fight with. I like that.

Industry observers note that zonveer sent me a ZX3 to test, and I’m impressed with what they shipped, knowing the cost. It isn’t trying to be a race bike. And it doesn’t need to be. Here’s my first ride review:.

With 2,800W peak, it’s somewhat modest by e-moto standards. That’s exactly what makes it approachable for someone who has never ridden a dirt bike: the power is enough to have a blast on trails without being intimidating.

My girlfriend had never ridden a dirt bike before, and she got comfortable within a few minutes, and she was hooked as soon as she got the hang of it.

Recent findings suggest that and while testing with my girlfriend, it was clear this bike makes the most sense for lighter riders. Zonveer claims it climbs slopes of up to 30 degrees, which is optimistic for anyone over ~175 lbs, like myself. It still climbed some of the worst slopes on my land, but it did so with some difficulty, which wasn’t the case for some of my lighter friends who also rode it.

Sources indicate that range is the other claim to take with a grain of salt. Riding 45 miles on 1,200Wh means using under 27Wh per mile, which is e-bike efficiency on a 130 lb dirt bike with knobby tires. It’s still a lot of energy, and you can ride this long distances at lower speeds. Just expect less if you ride it hard, and that’s where the fun is at.

Zonveer’s Black Friday sale has the ZX3 at $1,299, and the tech giant gave Electrek readers the code ELECTREK for an extra 5% off, which brings it down to $1,234.05.

It has been revealed that the sale also includes a free water bottle and lock, and can be combined for a two-pack of ZX3s for $2,599. Shipping is free, the warranty is one year, Zonveer told us it accepts returns within 30 days on bikes ridden less than 10 miles, with a $200 restocking fee. Here’s the full refund policy.

It has been revealed that we’ve ridden a lot of electric two-wheelers, and the ZX3 is one of the most fun per dollar. At $1,299, or about $1,234 with our code, it’s hard to find another 1,200Wh electric dirt bike with dual hydraulic disc brakes and full suspension from a brand that ships from US warehouses.

It’s not fast by e-moto standards, and the range and climbing claims are optimistic. But for beginners, and especially lighter riders, the power lands right in that sweet spot of manageable fun. It’s a bike you can learn on without scaring yourself, and it’s cheap enough that a family can buy two for less than one Sur-Ron.

Tesla kills $41,990 Model Y AWD: all-wheel drive now costs $8,000 more

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has pulled the $41,990 Model Y All-Wheel Drive from its US online configurator.
  • According to recent reports, the trim lasted just over nine months.
  • Here’s what Tesla’s US Model Y design studio lists as of today (prices before the destination fee):.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has pulled the $41,990 Model Y All-Wheel Drive from its US online configurator. The cheapest dual-motor Model Y you can order now is the Model Y Premium AWD at $49,990, an $8,000 jump.

According to recent reports, the trim lasted just over nine months. Tesla introduced it in early February, and it’s gone without a word from the manufacturer.

Here’s what Tesla’s US Model Y design studio lists as of today (prices before the destination fee):.

Sources indicate that when Tesla introduced the base Model Y AWD in February, it was basically the stripped-down Model Y with a second motor. It had 294 miles of range, did 0-60 mph in 4.6 seconds and kept the same cut-down cabin as the base RWD. At a $2,000 premium over the single-motor version, it was the most sensible AWD pricing Tesla had offered in years.

It has been revealed that and the AWD trim isn’t the only change. In February, the Premium RWD cost $44,990 and the Premium AWD cost $48,990. Both are now $1,000 higher.

Industry observers note that add it up and the cheapest all-wheel-drive Model Y went from $41,990 to $49,990 in nine months. That’s a 19% increase.

The timing isn’t great for Tesla’s competitive position. Chevrolet’s 2027 Equinox EV LT 1 AWD starts at $40,295 before destination, with 307 miles of EPA range. Ford’s Mustang Mach-E Select AWD starts at $40,795.

Both now undercut Tesla’s cheapest AWD crossover by more than $9,000.

If you live somewhere it snows and you were shopping for a new Model Y, the math just got a lot worse. You can still find some base AWD units in Tesla’s inventory, but once those are gone, that’s it.

Recent findings suggest that this is also the latest cut in a year of Tesla shrinking its lineup. Elon Musk killed the Model S and Model X in January to free up Fremont for Optimus, and Cybertruck production is winding down. Meanwhile, the most recent newly introduced Tesla is the $61,990 Model Y L, which sits at the top of the range, not the bottom.

Recent findings suggest that we liked this trim. It was the first time in a long time that Tesla treated all-wheel drive as a $2,000 option rather than a huge upsell bundled with a nicer interior, and it put the Model Y right in the price bracket of the Equinox EV and Mach-E with AWD.

Now it’s gone, and the Premium trims went up $1,000 on top of that. Tesla didn’t explain either move. It rarely does anymore.

There are two plausible reasons. Either Tesla is tight on Model Y build slots and would rather fill them with higher-margin Premium trims, or the cheap AWD simply wasn’t selling. We don’t know which. But both explanations land in the same place for buyers: a more expensive Model Y.

Recent findings suggest that tesla is not going to keep 6 different model Y trims especially when the most expensive trim in the Model YL is selling. They will definitely squeeze out as much money from selling more expensive trims so the lowest end trim will most likely be next to go.

In a recent development, and Tesla has a habit of this. The “Standard” name for its cheaper Model Y and Model 3 lasted a few months. The single-motor Cybertruck, the only version that made sense, was gone within days. Cheaper trims show up, get a news cycle, and quietly disappear.

That’s a problem for a firm whose consumer lineup is shrinking down to two cars. The Model Y is Tesla’s volume. Thinning it out at the bottom is the opposite of what you’d do if growing EV sales were the priority.

How long before the $39,990 RWD goes the same way?

#167131. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1083 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?
  • A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.
  • Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” noted study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

Sources indicate that A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” mentioned Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

It has been revealed that laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

It has been revealed that A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep challenges related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”.

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Sources indicate that additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

In a recent development, “This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”.

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein stated. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”.

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein stated.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”.

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

Sources indicate that “For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein stated. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”.

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

Industry observers note that “I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein remarked. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

In a recent development, the second major trucking deal between Facebook parent manufacturer Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 latest battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

“Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, noted Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”.

According to recent reports, meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This fresh Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The company adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy upcoming trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Healthline ↗ Open Full Page

ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.
  • Sources indicate that these expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date.
  • According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

Sources indicate that these expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include upcoming clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep complications, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

It has been revealed that “This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”.

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to recent reports, according to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

According to recent reports, A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies indicated some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

According to recent reports, it also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:.

Research indicates that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

Industry observers note that “This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” mentioned Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”.

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

It has been revealed that there are right now two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:.

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

Recent findings suggest that “Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document indicates what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” stated Pier.

Latest Update: Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase.
  • Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.
  • LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the tech giant has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the tech giant has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

In a recent development, the other massive piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

Industry observers note that GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

In a recent development, perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

Sources indicate that there’s an crucial caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T says it is currently fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Recent findings suggest that real Motors aims to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

It has been revealed that I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The tech giant demonstrated off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The upcoming models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha highlighted off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s new compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway revealed off a new vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

According to recent reports, the concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that the company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The newly introduced Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU highlighted off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The manufacturer indicated off several upcoming models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the organization has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

It has been revealed that with its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up upcoming possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no announced production plans, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A fresh Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

Breaking: Cheating on Food Intake: How, Why, and What to Do

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • At any given time, millions of American adults (and some younger) are on a diet.
  • Unfortunately, food cheating can lead to weight gain, failure to lose weight, and diet-disease consequences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 23, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

At any given time, millions of American adults (and some younger) are on a diet. That means they are watching their weight. Or trying to. Some diets actually incorporate “cheat days” or “cheat meals.” Some people on diets institute their own cheats—as in, “I’ll just splurge on this tonight, and get back to my diet tomorrow.”.

Unfortunately, food cheating can lead to weight gain, failure to lose weight, and diet-disease consequences.

Where does this come from? Is cheating a “thing” in its own right or does it have more to do with food cravings, impulse control, metabolism, brain function, gut health, and any number of other body and brain processes?

In a recent development, to take a closer look at this, we can check out research on people reporting their food intake. After all, that is the only way we can find out what people are eating. Or think they are eating.

How is this tracked? There are a variety of ways, including self-report questionnaires, 24-hour recall forms, recording food intake in the moment on an app, taking pictures of food being eaten, and wearing cameras throughout the day. There are some problems with all of these methods. For example, people may report differently when they are part of a study that watches what they eat. Still, there have been some discoveries that are fairly consistent.

People are not great at reporting what they eat. They typically underreport snack foods, readily available foods, and foods that are high-calorie and feel more rewarding than vegetables. Most commonly, people tend to forget the snacks they grab between meals. Interestingly, people also tend to overreport their intake of healthy foods, like proteins or vegetables.

Digging deeper, there are some nuances.

Social pressure can work both ways. If someone has unveiled to their family and friends that they are on a diet or following a certain initiative, they may feel pressure to eat only healthy items when in that group. On the other hand, some may just go along with a group if they are enjoying some party foods. Being observed versus not being observed may also be part of the mix.

Distraction can cause people to grab a food and forget about it.

Negative affect can be associated with emotional eating and giving in to the impulse to seek highly palatable foods, and then have it slip from their memories.

Memory and judgment complications: One study (2020) discovered that negative affect is associated with decreased memory suppression in the hippocampus of palatable food cues. In other words, palatable food cues become more salient and can lead to wanting those items.

Another study (2019) noted that the Western diet, which includes processed foods, can impact the hippocampus and several other areas to impair judgment.

It has been revealed that the hippocampus is a center of memory and can be implicated in confirmation bias. An article in the Washington Post (2022) noted that “one of the biggest problems to correcting information is the fact that hearing the truth doesn’t delete a falsehood from our memory.” Our brains store the original piece of misinformation, and it takes a different tagging system to get at the truth. To put it in the context of cheating with food, perhaps the eating was unconscious, or perhaps the person just doesn’t want to identify as a person who sneaks food. Either way, there is the memory that the cheat didn’t happen. The memory can become part of an identity or even a system of belief.

Metabolism: Excess weight can affect leptin signaling, so that hunger signals are inhibited, leading to food consumption unrelated to hunger signals.

Excess weight can lead to diabetes and insulin resistance. A study (2019) showed insulin resistance to be associated with deficits in episodic memory.

Recent findings suggest that one study (2023) used a trial of supervised machine learning, which did, in the end, mitigate food underreporting. Unfortunately, this is not a sustainable process, or one that could be used widely.

Sources indicate that another study (2015) used Inhibitory Control Training with some success. However, the gains they made were only short-term.

A study (2016) noted that accurate monitoring is “synonymous with the most weight loss.” However, studies that provide opportunity to do so are necessarily time-limited. The process needs to nurture long-term skills to maintain success.

Sources indicate that irregular eating patterns have been associated with cheating. So, one strategy would be to encourage people to eat regular meals and double down on planning.

Another strategy includes education or coaching. Awareness of the potential areas where pitfalls can happen and presenting other options may give people a strategy they can use long-term.

In a recent development, education could include some of the reasons why cheating is so prevalent. It’s not a moral failure. It’s human nature, and it’s the way our bodies work. Knowledge can start to make some inroads.

Monitoring is a good tool. It is an external process that can lead to awareness. However, the strategies above point to an overarching process that is internal—changing attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors. These are changes that can be realized over time and can be lasting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, your optimal sleep setup doesn’t have to be a fantasy. Over the past six years, the Shop AD team has tested dozens of options for our annual Sleep Week spotlight, so we can wax poetic about the difference between down and down alternative fills or the benefits of linen versus sateen duvet covers at length.

Industry observers note that year after year, the Brooklinen Down Comforter has been the all-around favorite on this list for its supple texture, even weight, breathability, and easy care instructions. The brand revamped the blanket in 2026, and we’re pleased to report that the new version is even better than the original based on our writers’ experiences. Beyond Brookinen’s award-winning model, we’re highlighting our full lineup of favorites in case something else is a better fit for your bedscape. The list includes lightweight picks when hot temperatures spike, heavyweight contenders for cold nights, and year-round eco-friendly comforters made with sustainably sourced materials.

Sources indicate that for consistency, the prices in this story reflect queen sizes. However, many brands offer options ranging from a twin to a king size.

The brand recommends using a commercial washer and dryer only for routine care.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve come to know Brooklinen very well over the years, and several of us have tried and loved their signature down comforter while testing their products. Contributor Rebecca Grambone calls the original “very high quality and luxurious” with “strong hotel bed vibes.”.

In a recent development, even though the down comforter never disappointed, the brand gave it an upgrade this year, and shopping writer Julia Harrison says it stacks up even better against the old version, citing “some notable upgrades.” For one thing, “they’ve upped the amount of fill in each and cloaked them in a sateen shell for coolness,” Harrison says. “They, thankfully, kept the easy-tie loops, not just in the four corners but the top and bottom as well, which work perfectly with their duvet covers.” The fill power only decreased for the lightweight offering (from 650 to 600), so it’s designed to feel even more cool and breathable if you sleep hot.

It has been revealed that technical stuff aside, Harrison says it “feels expensive,” notably from the fluffy and even baffle-box construction and the velvety sateen cover. “It even smells expensive: clean, fresh, unbothered,” she adds. “The feathers never poke out and stab me, which is a real issue with down on occasion, and I’ve had no issue having the cover stay in place.” Harrison has the all-season version to make her life easy (meaning she doesn’t have to switch it out or store it from season to season), and “it’s never too hot or too cold, and it’s easy to fluff up in the morning when I’m making my bed.”.

According to recent reports, our team has done a lot of research on Quince over the last year, and we’ve given the much-discussed brand’s linen duvet covers and bamboo sheets our seal of approval for their affordability and durability. So, naturally, we were excited to hear contributor Zoë Sessums’s praise of their goose down comforter. She noted that the price point is surprisingly low for such high-quality bedding (especially compared to competitors), and claims she would recommend it to anyone. Filled with European white goose down and available in both lightweight and all-season options, this down duvet insert is designed with double-stitched seams and a baffle-box construction to prevent lumps.

Boll & Branch has cracked the code for breathable, thoughtfully crafted and sustainable bedding. The retailer is conscientious with their approach to supply chain and holistic practices, earning Fair Trade and GOTS seals as well as Oeko-Tex certifications, which means you’re sleeping under something luxe that isn’t packed with microplastics.

Certifications aside, AD PRO senior editor Mel Studach can attest to this: The brand’s down insert has a 100% organic cotton shell that works as a breathable layer strong enough to keep the fills from poking through. “The duvet insert made a great first impression,” Studach says. “And with attachable corner loops, the insert was easy to situate within my Blu Dot duvet cover. The baffle-box construction keeps the down evenly distributed throughout the cover.” Studach recommends this for a year-round option if you like to keep your room cold and snuggle up. One last perk: The various weight options mean you can better personalize it to your sleep temperature preferences.

Because this is more of a quilt-comforter hybrid, our tester says she typically prefers blankets with a little more loft, or a fluffier feel to them.

Sources indicate that perhaps you prefer a generously sized blanket over a lofty comforter, or maybe you’re looking for a lighter weight bed topper instead of a chunky knit blanket. Whatever the case, senior shopping editor Nashia Baker says this is the perfect quilt-comforter hybrid. “I am always looking for some sort of two-in-one design element in my apartment whenever I can: I have a storage bed so I don’t have to conjure up some other place to put all my bulky blankets and clothes, a cooling pillow so I don’t have to crank my AC unless it’s absolutely necessary, you get the gist,” she says. “So the fact that I don’t need to have a separate duvet insert and cover in the mix is nice when I want a more simple bedspread.”.
